en: Record of the Commentary on the *Śāsanāntara-sūtra*, Scroll One (including the preface), composed by Guanfu of Xiaʼan.
This treatise, along with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and others, was all translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty in Nan Yue. Later, his younger brother...
Zi Zongkai and others wished to welcome him back to Jianye; however, fearing that those in Dangtu might seize his temporal prestige, they memorialized the throne and had the matter declined.
Consequently, the translations produced by the monks of Nanhai remained hidden during the Chen dynasty.

From the Chen through the Tang Kaiyuan era, there was only the title of this treatise, while the original text was missing. Later, when Zhisheng compiled the *Shijiao lu*, it was then finally obtained.
The root treatise (*śāstra-mūla*). Now, based on this treatise, the sūtras shall be categorized and included within the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.

Consequently, as the root treatise was previously lacking, ancient masters directly classified the sūtra as Hīnayāna. Only the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* consistently assigned the sūtra to the Mahāyāna.
Although contemporary authors possess this treatise as a guide, when it comes to judging the [status of the] sūtra as Mahāyāna...
The *Xiaozhuan* [Commentary] contains two or three [sections], likely because its author failed to examine the source and transmission [of the texts].

As for the *Shizhuan* [Commentary], it only relies on the *Zhufa* [Commentary] to expound the two records (*jì*). Although their methods of expounding and classifying the teachings differ, their explanations of the text are entirely copied from the *Zhufa*.

Examining the intent of the treatise now, the two records contain many errors; when cross-referenced and used to resolve the wording, they are again half right and half wrong. Since they cannot be accepted in their entirety...
Since it is neither possible to rely on [the text] exclusively nor to discard it entirely, I have adopted what was gained and discarded what was lost, compiling this into three fascicles.

I have recorded my own understanding directly and titled it the *Yijiao jing lun ji* (Record of the Commentary on the Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra). It is my hope that the literary intent of Aśvaghoṣa may, through this, provide some benefit for those who come after.
Written on the full moon of the second month in the Jiazi year of the Shaoxing era. Preface by the Abbot of the Huayan Pagoda Hall.
The commentary on this treatise is divided into three sections: first, the title; second, the homage; and third, the explanation of the text. Within the first section, there are two parts:

first, the heading of the title, which is explained according to six meanings: (1) a general clarification of the establishment of the title; (2) a specific elucidation of the treatise’s name; (3) a comparative analysis of its expansion and contraction;
(4) an explanation of the meaning of the terms; (5) a clarification through questions and answers; and (6) the determination of what is to be included or excluded. First...

In the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*), it is said: "Sometimes 'person' (*púruṣa*) is used as the heading; sometimes 'dharma' is used as the title. Regarding persons, there are distinctions such as those who request the teaching and so forth;

regarding dharmas, there are differences such as the dharma itself and its metaphors. Sometimes they refer to essence or function, sometimes to fruit or cause; appearing alternately complex or simple, their categories are manifold and extensive.
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shù*) adds 'the signifier and the signified,' or 'the true and the deluded, object and wisdom. Thus, in our school..."

The general designation "treatise" (*śāstra*) applies to many phenomena; regardless of which sūtra or treatise it concerns, or how a specific name is established, it is not restricted to a fixed definition. Second, to specifically clarify the categories of treatises:

there are two types of treatises. First, compendia of meaning (*piṇḍārtha-śāstra*), which collect and organize categories of meaning from within the sūtras to form a treatise, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Second, commentaries (*vyākhyāna-śāstra*), which explain the text according to a specific sūtra, such as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-bhāṣya*.
Regarding this treatise: for this reason, the title of this treatise is designated by means of the name of the sūtra it explains.

If one asks what is used as the designation among the "person," "dharmas," and so forth explained previously, if it is according to the title of the treatise, it receives its name based on that which is explained;
since that which is explained is the sūtra, it receives its name based on the teaching. If, however, it concerns the title of the sūtra being explained...

Regarding the analysis of what constitutes a "name": the teaching that is transmitted is the Dharma. The Dharma consists of doctrine, principle, practice, and fruit; this [teaching] is also the doctrine.

If one refers to the transmitter as a person, then "transmission" encompasses both the agent and the object, thereby including both person and Dharma. Regarding the analysis of the opening and closing of these three pairs:
the four characters proceed from the broad to the narrow through four layers of opening and closing. First is the character for "treatise" (*lun*); this is the general term for that which explains.

This is the title. Since it is customary to refer to a commentary as a "śāstra" (treatise), the first three characters are the specific designation for the sūtra being explained, as this work specifically comments upon the *Śāriputra-parivarta Sūtra* (the *Yijiao jing*) among all the sūtras.
This [title] possesses two pairs of designations: first, the relationship between the agent and the object, meaning that which explains and that which is explained;
second, the relationship between the general and the specific, meaning the general name and the specific name. Next, regarding these three characters, the sūtra is...

The "capable of expressing" (*abhilāpaka*) is the means of expression, while the "bequeathed teaching" (*śāsana*) is that which is expressed, for it is by means of this sutra that the bequeathed instructions are elucidated;

thus, there is the pair of "expression and intended meaning. Next, regarding the first two characters: "teaching" (*śāsana*) refers specifically to the Dharma that was bequeathed, and is therefore restricted to the "object" (*lakṣya*); whereas "bequeathed" (*avaśeṣita*) applies to both the subject and the object, and thus constitutes the pair of "the general and the specific.
Therefore, this single title unfolds four pairs through its various combinations. Fourth, as for the explanation of the meaning of the name: "Bequeathed Teaching" (*Yijiao*).
Thus, "entrusting" (*parindanā*) is taken as the name, while "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) constitutes its meaning. The *Zhufa ji* (Record of Abiding in the Dharma) states:

"The 'Bequeathed Teaching' has two senses: first, the entrustment of subsequent affairs; second, the final testament at the time of death. Therefore, when the following treatise explains the phrase "after my parinirvāṇa," it says:

"These words manifest the meaning of the Bequeathed Teaching"; this refers to the first sense. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the "final instruction," it says: "This precisely reveals the Bequeathed Teaching."

"Meaning" (yi) refers to the subsequent meaning; it refers to the six sections of the main body of the scripture (*zhengzong*), which provide instructional admonitions by pointing to specific matters and are intended for future generations, such as worldly testaments.
"Sūtra" (*jing*) is named for its capacity to express [the truth], and its essential function is to thread together and encompass [the teachings].
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it can penetrate (*pāṭana*) and because it can collect (*saṃgraha*), it is called a Sūtra.

This is because the holy teachings of the Buddha penetrate and maintain the meanings that ought to be explained for the sake of those to be converted. Regarding the term "Śāstra," it is named according to its function as an explanation; "to analyze" (*vibhañjana*) is its meaning.

That is to say, it evaluates the principles of the teachings and analyzes terminology; therefore, it is called a Śāstra. Fifth, regarding "clarification through question and answer": [Question: This...
Regarding the title of this treatise: is it intended to indicate the title of the sūtra by quoting it in full, or is it intended to indicate the title of the sūtra by quoting it in brief?
Answer: It may be either full or brief. Why is this so? If the word "Buddha" does not appear at the beginning of the sūtra’s title, it is a brief name;
if the word "Buddha" is added at the beginning, it is a full name. Now, examining the sūtra in its Tripitaka edition, it correctly bears the title *The Buddha’s Imminent Parinirvāṇa*.

The *Nirvāṇa-saṃkṣiptopadeśa-sūtra*. According to the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, based on the records of Sengyou, it is also called the *Buddha’s Final Words* (*Fo lin ban*) and the first is titled the *Śāsana-avaśeṣa-sūtra*.
In the *Neidian Lu*, it has alternative titles, being also called simply the *Śāsana-avaśeṣa-sūtra*. Other catalogs of scriptures list only its formal title.
As for the versions currently circulating in the world and those commented upon by the ancient masters, they are all referred to as: [the *Yijiao jing*].
Regarding the *Buddha-śāsana-avaśeṣa-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching), both the old and new catalogs of the canon lack the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) at the beginning.

This should be understood as stated in the *Zhufa ji* (Record of the Abiding Dharma): that the character "Buddha" was added by later generations. Xuanxian agrees with this; thus, this explanation is correct. Question:

The various masters who preceded you all explained the title with the character "Buddha" at the beginning. Why do you not follow them now? Answer: This is like the case of [the title of] the *Amitābha*... [text ends].
In the Tripitaka manuscripts and various catalogs, the phrase "spoken by the Buddha" (佛說) is entirely absent; yet, in the versions widely circulated in the world, it is frequently present.
Even the commentaries on the titles by masters such as Dàshèngfǎshī explain this very phrase.

Since it is missing from both the Tripitaka manuscripts and the catalogs, it is clear that later generations added it. However, because the former virtuous masters lacked access to the Tripitaka catalogs, they too provided an explanation for it.

Furthermore, prior to the Zhenyuan era, titles of translated scriptures generally lacked the phrase "spoken by the Buddha" (佛說). However, in the titles of newly translated scriptures from the Zhenyuan period onward, the characters for "Buddha" and so forth are frequently included.
Could it be that the Sanskrit manuscripts of the older translations mostly lacked this, while those of the newer translations mostly contained it?
By examining this, one knows that these are merely the result of the translators' own intentions. When this scripture was translated by Master Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin period, since...
The two names, "Zheng" (Correct) and "Bie" (Separate), constitute one name as a complete term and one name as an abbreviated term. Question: The *Zhufa ji* states:

"Now, examining secular classics, it is not necessary to prefix the word 'Buddha' [to the title], because within a great trichiliocosm, the final legacy of the teachings is that which was spoken by a single Buddha."
This [title] alone refers exclusively to the Honored One; therefore, it is not explicitly marked here, as there is nothing to be excluded.

However, as for why the word "Buddha" was included in the formal title of the preceding section, it is intended to show that the words spoken at the time of passing into parinirvāṇa are linked to the name of the person [who spoke them], unlike other sutras which exclude what was said by others.
What does this mean? The answer is: this explanation, on the contrary, invites a difficulty. Why? For instance, if someone were to raise an objection: "If one simply says 'bequeathed'..."
Question: Regarding the other teachings, when looking at those of the non-Buddhists and others at the time of their death, do they not leave behind instructions?

They themselves say these are like what is called a "testament" in the world; thus, there would be confusion within the title. Therefore, the main title first displays the character "Buddha. Furthermore, it is objected:

If it is claimed that the word "Buddha" (佛) serves to distinguish [the teaching] from the words "imminent parinirvāṇa" (垂般), this is because the term "imminent parinirvāṇa" applies generally to other sages as well;

therefore, one speaks of using the word "Buddha" to select [this specific case]. Furthermore, since the "imminent parinirvāṇa," the "brief exposition," and the "instruction" are all [taught by] the Buddha, how could they be distinguished by being pervaded [by the title] throughout?

Thus, one should know that [such an argument] conversely invites a logical difficulty. Question: If the word "Buddha" were absent, would one not still be subject to this difficulty? Answer: As stated above: "It is said..."

All [titles] are translations of the original author’s intent; they do not claim to represent existence or non-existence. This is because of the distinction between being confused and not being confused.

Among the titles of other sutras, those that are confused are very numerous (as can be seen from the catalogs of the scriptures). If we take similar cases as examples, such as the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which has two translations from the same original:
one version does not record the translator's name and its title is simply *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*; another version was translated by Bai Fazhu of the Western Jin, and its title...

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa," there is likewise a distinction between the full and abbreviated forms. It should not lack the word "Buddha," for otherwise it would be confused with the parinirvāṇa of other sages.

If one were to say that omitting it still leads to confusion, then since the titles of most scriptures translated during the Jin and Han dynasties frequently do not include the word "Buddha" and so forth, they would all be subject to such confusion.
Thus, we know that this depends solely on the intention of the translator. Now, although Master Kumārajīva’s two titles [of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*] are complete...

The distinction between the abbreviated and the full versions is also like that of the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which exists in two translations from the same original, possessing both the full and abbreviated titles.

Furthermore, since the term "leaving behind" (*yí*) applies to both the agent and the object, its meaning encompasses the Buddha who leaves behind. Sixth, regarding the determination of what to include or exclude:

the fact that the Tibetan version uses "the Buddha about to enter parinirvāṇa" and so forth as a general heading is because Master Kumārajīva’s translation intended to establish the correct nomenclature.
The treatise is easily identified by its distinct title. Furthermore, as human nature favors brevity, the *Shiben* (Genealogy of the World) records only this name.

Thus, the translators of the treatise followed this worldly convention and abbreviated the title. Consequently, while Ratnamati’s full translation of the *Fahua shilun* is titled the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Lun*, Bodhiruci’s abbreviated translation is simply called the *Fahua Jing Lun*.
Thus, one knows that the fullness or brevity of a title depends upon the translator. Now, this treatise follows the abbreviated version.
Regarding the two translators: as for Aśvaghoṣa, tradition says there was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) of great wisdom in Central India who did not permit the public sounding of the *ghanṭā* (gong).
When [Aśvaghoṣa] sounded it and came to seek a debate on the meaning of the doctrines, at that time the Venerable Pārśva was traveling from Northern India to visit Central India.

Zhú struck the *gaṇḍī* (the upper character is pronounced *jù hán*; the lower is pronounced *dì*, referring to a type of bell or chime). The non-Buddhist practitioner arrived at the site of the debate. Pārśva’s commentary states:
"Now that the world is in great peace, the Great King enjoys longevity, the four lands are prosperous and flourishing, and there are no calamities or afflictions.
The non-Buddhist was thus defeated and became his disciple. Later, the King of Kṣudra-Mahāśaka (pronounced *zhī*) intended to test him.
Because he practiced the True Dharma, he requested that the essentials of the Dharma be preached.

Having fasted for seven days, when the True Dharma was being preached, he led the horse into the assembly and gave it *pūlī* grass (the horse eats *pūlī* grass, therefore it was given to it). The horse would not eat at all;

instead, it neighed piteously and shed tears while listening attentively to the essentials of the Dharma. For this reason, he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigher). According to the *Dharmakośasaṃgraha*, Pūrṇayaśas [was like] a horse.
Ming engaged in debate. Once Ming was defeated, Śaradvat left the household life. Ming, however, remained unconvinced and intended to sacrifice his life.

Śaradvat immediately entered meditative concentration and perceived Ming’s thoughts. At that time, there was already a scripture within the dark room; he then said to Ming, "Go and fetch the scripture.
Ming replied, "This room is pitch black; how can I go to fetch it? Śaradvat said, "Just go, and you shall see it now."
At that time, Śrī used his supernormal powers to extend his right hand from afar into the dark chamber, emitting light from his five fingers.

Its radiance was so brilliant that Mingyou (Ming-yu) was thereby moved to submit as his disciple. According to tradition, he was the disciple of Pārśva; according to the *Dharmakośa-āgama* (or *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*), he was the disciple of Upagupta.

He was the disciple of Śrī (Śa). Since Xiā (脇) was the ninth patriarch and Śrī was the tenth, it is feared that both were disciples of two different individuals, and thus their lineages branched out separately; hence they are not the same. The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"When this Bodhisattva was first born, he moved all the horses so that they neighed incessantly. Furthermore, he was skilled at playing the lute to proclaim the sound of the Dharma. All the horses...
Upon hearing this, they all let out mournful neighs. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* mentions six "horse-neighers" (*aśvaghoṣas*). There are differing accounts in the sūtras:

the *Jinzheng jing* states that seventeen days after the Buddha attained enlightenment, a non-Buddhist named Aśvaghoṣa appeared and challenged the Buddha; the *Maṇiviśuddhi-sūtra* says he appeared one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; the *Nirmāṇaguṇa-sūtra* says he appeared three hundred years later;

the *Māyā-sūtra* says he appeared six hundred years later; the *Dhruvaguṇasamādhi-sūtra* says eight hundred years later; and the *Vyūhasamādhi-sūtra* states that in the past there was a bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa. According to the original source, he is none other than Mahāprabha.

Regarding "Mingfo" (Faming): if one clarifies his cause, he is a Bodhisattva of the Eighth Stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). In reference to the realm of those to be converted, he is designated by the name of the person who converts them;

thus, because he followed the neighing of a horse, he is called "Maming" (Horse-Neigh). As for the term "Bodhisattva," it is fully *bodhisattva*, which here means "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*), as explained in the usual commentaries.
Regarding the word "author" (*zuo*), the *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*) states in its extensive citations: "The author."
"Composed" (*kṛta*) refers to its being newly produced; "narrated" (*nirukta*) refers to its having existed previously.
Regarding the statement "translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha," tradition says his name was Kuḷanātha, which in the Chen language means "Reliance" (*pratiśaraṇa*);
alternatively, he was called Paramārtha, which means "Ultimate Truth. Both are names from the Sanskrit original. He was originally from Ujjayinī in Western India.

A native of Nīla, he arrived at Jianye in the second year of the Daqing era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty. As the Liang state was then collapsing in chaos, he was unable to propagate his teachings.
Later, observing the conditions of the land, he intended to cross the sea to go to Laṅkāśaila to repair his kingdom; however, both monastics and laypeople entreated him to remain.
He subsequently stayed in Nan Yue. Later, he set sail westward from Liang’an, but driven by an adverse wind and his allotted fate, he was cast back to Guangzhou.

The Regional Inspector, Duke Ou-yang Mu (Wei), invited him to reside at Chih-chi Temple and requested that he translate the *Fa-men ching* (Dharmamukha-sūtra), the *Wei-shih lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra), and other texts.
After Duke Mu passed away, his heir, Hsüeh-ho, again requested that he transmit these scriptures. His spiritual insight was profound and penetrating, and his capacity was beyond measure.

Qingce usually resided in a separate place on an island cut off from the four directions by water. Xi went to visit him; however, the mountain ridges were steep and the waves surged, so he did not dare to venture across.
Tidi then spread out his sitting mat upon the water and sat cross-legged within it as if riding in a boat. He floated over the waves and reached the shore.
Once they had met and were seated together, the sitting mat was not even damp. His divine wonders were numerous in such instances. Later, his disciple Zong...

When Huikai and others wished to escort Paramārtha back to Jianye, the eminent scholars and officials of Yangzhou feared that he would usurp their contemporary prestige; they thereupon submitted a memorial stating:

"The various sections translated in the regions south of the passes mostly elucidate 'dustless consciousness-only' (vimala-vijñaptimātra). These doctrines deviate from the arts of governance and will corrupt the national character."

He did not belong among the various Han Chinese, yet he was able to spread [the Dharma] throughout the remote borderlands. The Emperor agreed with this. Thus, his new writings from the Nanhai region were preserved during the Chen dynasty.
In the first year of the Taian era, he fell ill; at noon on the eleventh day of the first month, he passed away. He was seventy-one years of age.

From the second year of Yongding of Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty (the wuyin year) until the first year of Taajian of Emperor Xiaodian (the jichou year), he retranslated thirty-eight works, including the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
As for the remaining untranslated texts, the Sanskrit manuscripts were all written on *tāla* leaves and totaled two hundred and forty bundles (*jiǎ*).
If these had been translated using Chinese paper, they would have amounted to more than twenty thousand fascicles.

The present translations have now been completed; these constitute merely a small portion. The remainder are all located in the two monasteries of Zhizhi and Wangyuan. Regarding the term "translator" (*yi*), the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song* states:

"In the *Rites of Zhou*, there were the 'Elephant-Script' for communicating with the six Man tribes; the 'Di-di' official oversaw the seven Rong tribes; the 'Si' official was charged with the nine Yi tribes; and the 'Yi' official understood the eight Di tribes.
Now, among the various offices of the four quarters, why is it that only the office of the Translator is so prominent? It has been since the Han dynasty..."
Since ancient times, [this region] has mostly dealt with matters of the North; therefore, it was translated as "Lànshú" (爛熟).
Furthermore, regarding the act of translating, it is like translating brocade: both sides are beautiful, though their patterns differ on the left and right.

Consequently, these two types of translation have been practiced. However, there are four possibilities: first, translating the characters but not the phonetics, such as *dhāraṇī*; second, translating the phonetics...

First, there are characters that are not translated, such as the *svastika* on the Buddha’s chest. Second, there are characters where both the sound and the meaning are translated, such as the various Chinese terms found throughout the sutras.
Third, there are characters where neither the sound nor the meaning is translated, such as the first two characters of a sutra title.

Nevertheless, in antiquity it was universally said that "the Hu (foreign) was translated into Han (Chinese). By the Sui and Tang dynasties, however, it was commonly said that "Sanskrit was translated into Hua (Chinese). Therefore, I shall provide a comprehensive analysis here.

"Brahman" (*bàn*) and "Hu" (*hú*) are distinct. It should not be that those of antiquity all spoke of "Hu-language. From the Sui to the Tang dynasties, they all referred to it as "Brahman-language" (*fànyǔ*).
One must distinguish between the meanings of "Hu" and "Brahman" for the interpretation to be correct, as is detailed in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song).

Second, the section on taking refuge, paying homage, and requesting empowerment. First, the prostrations to the Three Jewels to whom one takes refuge. The first verse is for the Buddha; the second verse is for the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Regarding the reason for taking refuge in the Three Jewels, the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states that there are briefly six intentions:

first, because they bear the debt of their grace and virtue; second, to request their protective empowerment; third, to cause faith to arise; fourth, as a formal ritual; and fifth, to signify their supreme excellence.
Therefore, [the term] "six" refers to manifesting the benefit of sentient beings. The two characters for "prostration" (*namas*) signify the utmost sincerity of taking refuge;

that is, using one's own supreme crown to pay homage at the other's lowest feet—hence it is called "prostration. This represents the height of reverence. Now, in the Western Regions (India), there are nine types of salutation:
first, speaking words of inquiry; second, bowing the head to show respect; third, raising the hands with a gentle nod; fourth, joining the palms... [and so forth].

1. Prostration with hands joined; 2. Bowing with palms together; 3. Bowing with palms at the heart; 4. Bowing with palms at the forehead; 5. Bending the five limbs (kneeling); 6. Kneeling with the body upright; 7. Resting the head and elbows on the ground; 8. Placing all five wheels (limbs) on the ground; 9. Casting the entire body to the ground. We are now at the eighth.
As for the term "prostrating with the crown" (*namas-kāra*), if the crown touches the ground, it necessarily implies that both hands and knees do not fail to touch the ground as well;

thus, by mentioning the crown, the other four wheels are subsumed. Regarding the phrase "the three worlds," this refers to the scope of those to whom one takes refuge. It says "three... [to indicate the three times].

Regarding "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*): if one speaks of the World-Honored One alone, it refers specifically to his title as the Sole Honored One within the three realms, which is one of the ten epithets.
Therefore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the seventh and eighth [epithets] are combined into one, termed "Unsurpassed Great Being and Tamer of Men.

Thus, the title "World-Honored One" corresponds specifically to the tenth epithet. However, if considered collectively, he is honored by the world because he possesses the aforementioned ten virtues. Therefore—
The Unsurpassed One (*anuttara*) is the seventh; the Tamer of Men (*puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) is the eighth.

Thus, the Buddha constitutes the tenth, whereby the World-Honored One (*bhagavat*) possesses all ten titles in their entirety. Now, since the verse refers to the "World-Honored One of the three times," there are two senses of "three times":
first, within the three times of past, present, and future, the Buddha alone is most venerable; second, the two kinds of worlds, namely the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
The receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), and the world of the perfectly awakened ones (*jñānasambuddhaloka*).

Among these three worlds, because only the Buddha is most venerable, although the primary meaning extends vertically through the three periods of time, it in fact also encompasses horizontally the ten directions. When the three times are defined by time, time has no separate substance.

It is explained by way of its location; therefore, it necessarily encompasses the ten directions. Regarding the phrase "ocean of unsurpassed merit," because the Buddha’s virtues transcend all things, they are called "unsurpassed merit.
He possesses marks and embellishments as numerous as motes of dust, which are profound, vast, and immeasurable.

Therefore, it is likened to the ocean. This corresponds to what is said in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "The Tathāgata’s unsurpassed ocean of merit universally manifests as a bright lamp that illuminates the world;
all sentient beings are rescued and protected, and all are granted happiness without exception.

Herein, the first phrase corresponds to the second phrase of the present text; the second phrase corresponds to the first phrase above; and the final two phrases correspond to the third phrase of the present text.
To speak of "compassionately delivering sentient beings" refers to the salvation of all things through great kindness and compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*). "Delivering" (*tāraṇa*) signifies rescuing;
it is the Buddha’s compassion that acts as the power capable of delivering, while the sentient beings submerged in the depths of suffering are those to be delivered.

This means emerging from the ocean of the two deaths and reaching the shore of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Observe how the Dharma of the Tathāgata is ever thus: all sentient beings..."
Benefit. By the power of great loving-kindness and compassion, he can rescue those who are submerged in the perilous paths.

Now, regarding the first three characters of the first line of the verse of refuge, they collectively enumerate all virtues; the second line refers to "great wisdom," and the third line refers to "great compassion.
Since compassion and wisdom constitute the Buddha’s fundamental intention, these are set forth here to express the nature of that which is revered. Thus it says: "Therefore, I take refuge..."
The term "namas" (homage) is used to demonstrate respect. The first two syllables [of the word *namas*] signify that I welcome the Buddha, who is endowed with both compassion and wisdom;

therefore, I take refuge in him. The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "To 'take refuge' (*namas*) means to rely upon, to surrender oneself, and to direct one's course toward [the object]. 'Life-force' (*jīva*) refers to that which governs all the sense faculties; it is the essential core of the body.
Among all that is precious to a person, there is nothing more fundamental than this. By offering up this peerless life-force, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed One."

This is the meaning of "honoring. Furthermore, "returning" (gui) carries the sense of returning to the source. The six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of sentient beings arise from the one mind, yet they turn their backs on their own source and rush toward the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Now, by taking up the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), one comprehensively gathers the six emotions and returns them to the one mind.

This one mind is precisely the single essence of the Triple Gem (*triratna*). Question: Since the *Awakening of Faith* takes the one mind as its primary tenet, it possesses a sequential order of practice. Why is this [text] cited here? Answer:
The person capable of taking refuge is the Master of the Treatise, an eighth-stage Bodhisattva; how could he not have attained single-mindedness?
Moreover, the subsequent explanation of "single-mindedness" is also interpreted in terms of the mind of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*).
In the following verse, the first line refers to the Jewel of the Dharma; the second line refers to the Jewel of the Saṃgha; and the fourth line expresses the characteristic of taking refuge.
Regarding the phrase "the pure and profound dharmadhātu," this refers to the *dharmadhātu* in terms of principle (*li*). "Dhātu" carries the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*).

As for the description "pure and profound," this is because the dharmadhātu attained by Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles is not yet utterly pure nor has it reached its ultimate source; only the Buddha has thoroughly and completely penetrated it.

Because it is ultimately pure, it is distinguished by the profound term "pure. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It is called the 'Most Pure Dharmadhātu' because it distinguishes itself from the dharmadhātu attained by those of the two vehicles.
(The two interpretations in the *Zhufa ji* are both contrary to the intent of the treatise; they are excessively forced, especially since some have even recorded them as such).

This phrase, together with the preceding verse, constitutes the three bodies of the Buddha. Furthermore, the Three World-Honored Ones encompass both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body).

The body is honored as being equal to sentient beings across the three worlds, which pertains to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). If it refers to the Honored One throughout the three periods of past, present, and future, it pertains to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
As for that ocean of unsurpassed merit, it refers exclusively to the *saṃbhogakāya*, which out of compassion delivers sentient beings.

It also refers to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is because it crosses over the ocean of the two types of death. Bodhisattvas cross over the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmikī-jarāmaraṇa*);

this is based on the fact that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they perceive the reward body (*vipākakāya*). From this, the transformation body can be understood. What is here called the "pure and profound *dharmadhātu*" is precisely the *dharmakāya*.
If that is so, this is the Dharma Jewel; why then is it called the Buddha-body? Answer: Since this is the principle-dharmadhātu, it is also the fruition-dharma.
Because it is the profound dharmadhātu realized by the Buddha, it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If that is so, how can the two sections of the Buddha-dharma be correlated with the three bodies?
Answer: This follows the structural model of the *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith). That treatise states: "And that body..."
The essence and characteristics [of the Buddha] are the ocean of the *dharmatā* and *tathatā*. The Commentary states: "This is the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

Because the teaching is shallow while the principle is profound, and because practice is partial while the fruit is complete, one takes refuge in the principle and the fruit. Within the Greatness of Function, the two bodies of the Buddha—the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—are distinguished;

therefore, the two greatnesses of essence and characteristics are themselves the *dharmakāya* and are subsumed under the Jewel of the Dharma. What is now called the "pure and profound *dharmadhātu*" is itself the *dharmakāya*.

The meaning [of this passage] extends to both principle and its fruit, and thus it is subsumed under the Jewel of the Dharma; therefore, the text is located within the section on the Jewel of the Dharma, and its meaning corresponds to the Dharmakāya.
Question: Now that you speak of the "Dharmakāya," how do we know that this is indeed the Dharmakāya? Answer: In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (the *She lun*), the root treatise states:
"Furthermore, the Dharmadhātu of all Buddhas should at all times possess five activities. The commentary (*Śāstra*) explains: "This clarifies the activity of the Dharmakāya. And...

Regarding the statement "the dharma-dhātu of all Buddhas," it is intended to reveal that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) encompasses five meanings of the dharma-dhātu—namely, (1) the meaning of nature, (2) the meaning of cause, (3) the meaning of treasury, (4) the meaning of reality, and (5) the meaning of profundity—and thus it is renamed "dharma-dhātu. Therefore, one should know that the dharma-dhātu is itself the Dharma-body.

Although the dharma-dhātu fully subsumes these five meanings, they are all spoken of in reference to the *principle* dharma-dhātu (*li-fajie*). (The correlation of these with the three bodies and so forth, as found in the *Erji*, differs from this thesis; let the wise examine this carefully.)
The two phrases beginning with "increase" refer to the Jewel of the Saṃgha. There are two types of cultivation: first, that of one's own level (*svabhāga*);

second, that of advancement (*viśeṣagamana*). The present term "increase" refers specifically to advancement. This applies universally to the noble ones (*ārya*) of the three vehicles. The word "this" (*yaḥ*) serves to cite the person [who possesses these qualities].
Regarding "the mundane and the supramundane," this refers to those who practice the path of advancement in the supramundane realm, whether belonging to the three vehicles...

The middle three [stages] consist of the ordinary beings and the ten stages of the noble ones (śaikṣa); these are the mundane *saṃgha*. The four fruits and the ten stages of the noble ones (ārya) constitute the supramundane *saṃgha*.
To speak more precisely, the first three fruits are also considered mundane *saṃgha*, as they have not yet exhausted the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Regarding the phrase "I and others all take refuge (*namas*)," the *Xuanyan ji* states that the text contains two meanings. First, concerning the object of refuge, there are two interpretations. The first...
This means that because the Buddha’s virtues are uniquely extraordinary, he must be explained separately; whereas the meanings of the Dharma and the Sangha are equal, they are shown together.
Thus it says, "equally all. Second, regarding the two vehicles—Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—the Sangha Jewel, whether ordinary or noble, mundane or supramundane, is equally and universally taken as refuge.
Thus it says, "equally all. Second, regarding the subject who takes refuge: this means that by means of myself alone, I encompass all beings, and all of them take refuge.

Therefore it is said: "We all take refuge" (the former [text] explains this). Question: If that is so, since everything is now subsumed under taking refuge in the Dharma and the Saṃgha, why does the Jewel of the Buddha alone say, "I take refuge"?
Answer: Because the wording is abbreviated. Thus, the "I" mentioned briefly in the preceding [text] is implied here;
therefore, one should know that the "I" mentioned in the former [text] also subsumes all sentient beings and so forth.
All return to the Buddha. Question: For what reason are all things subsumed within taking refuge? Answer: It is because all Buddhas of the ten directions are filled with joy;
all Saṃghas of the ten directions offer praise; and the entire treasury of Dharma in the ten directions is perpetually disseminated.
Question: The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa had realized the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi). Regarding the merits of the lower grounds:
All are fully satisfied. Why is this? Because those in the lower stations all take refuge [in the higher]. Answer:

This is because the persons who are gathered and who take refuge are themselves identical to the station [of the object of refuge] (the preceding questions and answers are all based on the *Śāstra on the Mahāyāna*). As for the term *namas*, in the Sanskrit language it is correctly pronounced *vandana*;

this translates as "I pay homage. In meaning, it signifies "taking refuge in life" (*prāṇa-namaskāra*). However, when referring to the Buddha, one says "taking refuge in life"; for the Dharma and the Saṃgha, one says "namas."
None. This is merely a mutual citation between the Chinese and Sanskrit versions.

Second, the exposition of the original intent has two parts. Regarding the section beginning with "Discussing what belongs to the self," the first part correctly presents the intent. Now, as for the reason why one takes refuge in the Triple Gem:
I pray that you will bestow your majestic power upon me to explain these Buddhist scriptures.

This is so that bodhisattvas practicing in the final age may understand this path of skillful means, whereby the Buddha-dharma may endure for a long time, remaining free from calamities and bringing about great benefit. Regarding the statement "I": Question:

Since Aśvaghoṣa has already attained the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and both forms of self-grasping have been severed, why does he refer to himself as "I"? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In accordance with worldly conventions, one speaks of 'I'."

The self is not spoken of within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for all phenomena are in reality without self. Within the worldly conventions (*lokadharma*), there is no fault in speaking of a self.
Furthermore, worldly language has three roots: first, falsehood; second, pride; and third, names. The first two are impure, while the last one is pure.
All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess all three types of speech, whereas those on the path who have seen or cultivated [the truths] possess two types.
"Speech" refers to the speech that designates names; it is the single kind of speech used by the noble ones, namely, names.

Within their inner minds, they do not conceive of them as real dharmas, yet they follow worldly people in transmitting these words. Because the Buddha’s disciples conform to worldly custom, there is no fault in speaking of "I.
Now, in accordance with worldly custom, we say "I. Furthermore, the *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* states: "In the Western Regions and the South Seas, one says 'I' [to refer to oneself]. It does not...
This is a term of modesty. Even if it were said of you, it would not be a disparaging reference;
rather, it is intended to distinguish between "self" and "other," so as to prevent a sense of arrogance and ensure that one does not regard the land of China as inferior or base.

Based on this, the translator followed the customs of the Western Regions, which is why the sutra frequently uses the first-person pronoun "I. Regarding the phrase "establishing the treatise" (*śāstra-prasthāna*), it means to initiate and establish this treatise.
This is because it explains the Buddha’s sūtras; this is still the general meaning. It is only for the latter two lines that the specific meaning is established.

Nevertheless, if one reads through the text of this sūtra as a whole, it appears to be dedicated exclusively to the Hīnayāna; therefore, the masters of old, within their classifications of the Piṭakas and Vehicles, [categorized it accordingly].
All [of these] are included within the Hīnayāna. It is precisely for this reason that the Master of the Treatise, through his own wisdom, deeply understood the Buddha’s intention:

when the Buddha was on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, he preached this sūtra specifically for a certain class of Mahāyāna practitioners of shallow capacity who were unable to directly receive the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
His intent lay in the Mahāyāna, though the phrasing resembled that of the Hīnayāna; he foresaw the future...
Successive generations have failed to understand the Buddha’s intent; they have taken the text as it stands and categorized it within the Hīnayāna (Śrāvaka) teachings.
Consequently, those bodhisattvas practicing in the final age who lack sufficient intellectual power do not recognize this as the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna, and thus abandon this sutra.

Therefore, the Master of the Treatise established this treatise to ensure that they know this sutra is precisely the skillful means of the Mahāyāna, which merely incorporates [the Śrāvaka path] concurrently.
Regarding the Two Vehicles: this is why it specifically states, "for the sake of those bodhisattvas, so that they may know the path of skillful means.

As the subsequent text says, "Furthermore, it reveals the Mahāyāna path of skillful means shared with the Two Vehicles. This is the Master of the Treatise’s specific intention in explaining the meaning of the Sūtra.
Later commentators were unable to bring forth this principle, resulting in a dual confusion regarding both the Sūtra and the Treatise. If...
This sutra clarifies that it is intended for those with the profound capacity of the Mahāyāna, directly expounding the practices of Bodhisattvas, and does not concurrently include the Two Vehicles.
Any reader will naturally recognize for themselves that this sutra is a Mahāyāna scripture; how could the ancient masters have collectively classified it as a Hīnayāna work?
Only by using this treatise to explain it can one finally know that it is indeed Mahāyāna. The profound and hidden meaning of the text is specifically set forth here;
it awaits this treatise before becoming clear. Since this commentary reveals the deep intent of the Master of the Treatise, I hope there will be no further confusion.

Furthermore, after the verse of homage in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the Master also sets forth the purpose for composing the treatise, saying: "It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon..."

[This work] causes those with false attachments to give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. Since this is the fundamental treatise of the true teaching of the Mahāyāna,
Nāgārjuna’s commentary states that it enables all immeasurable sentient beings— whether non-Buddhists, ordinary worldlings, followers of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas—
to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments, and to proceed with resolute diligence toward the profound, correct path of the Mahāyāna.

Because it enters into dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it ensures that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted. The intent of this treatise is that it is a commentary on the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Since the sūtras it explains are often regarded as Hīnayāna by many in the final age, the Great Being (the author) foresaw this and specifically stated that it is "for those bodhisattvas" so that they may know the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), whereby the Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time. By contrast, this [Hīnayāna] treatise is not such.
Thus, being ignorant of skillful means (*upāya*), one mistakenly adopts the Hīnayāna, and the Buddha-dharma will swiftly perish. Question:

If that is so, then could it not be that by rejecting the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, one instead gives rise to faith in the Hīnayāna? Answer: Not so. If one were to reject that treatise, one would merely have a vague faith in the Mahāyāna;
one would be unable to give rise to correct faith within the profound and correct path of the Mahāyāna. It is precisely because of...
Regarding this meaning, that commentary specifically states: "It gives rise to firm faith because it brings certainty regarding the profound and correct path of the Mahāyāna.
This treatise, however, merely states that it causes one to know the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna path.

Thus, we know that if it were not for that [other] treatise, the provisional and the real would remain undifferentiated; yet if it were not for this treatise, one would not know that this sutra is the skillful means of the Mahāyāna. However, that...

This is the true teaching of the Mahāyāna; therefore, the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) refers to it as the "right path of the Mahāyāna. This [present work] is the provisional teaching of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, the present treatise refers to it as the "path of skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna. By comparing these two treatises, it is clear that there are two aspects to the Mahāyāna:

first, the right path, which is the true teaching; second, the path of skillful means, which corresponds to the provisional teaching. This is intended to clarify the provisional and the real nature of these two treatises.

Because of these differences, [the commentators] have all clarified their respective intentions following the verses of homage. These six sections of the orthodox tradition all reveal the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Mahāyāna;

when compared with that [other system], the meaning is self-evident. Yet, in the *Zhufa ji* (Record of Abiding in the Dharma), how much error has been committed in interpreting the words "skillful means" and so forth as indicating the provisional returning to the real? If this is what you all practice, then it is so.

To claim that the Bodhisattva path involves "transforming the small into the great" and causing those of the Two Vehicles to know skillful means (*upāya*) is entirely contrary to the intent of this treatise.

Furthermore, if it were the case that the provisional immediately returns to the real, then there would be only the One Vehicle; it should not be stated later that it is "shared with the Two Vehicles," as this would still belong to the category of shared teachings.
Moreover, how would this differ from the *Lotus Sūtra*’s assembly on skillful means? This [interpretation] lacks any point of contact with the text. If...
Xuanyan merely states: "It is intended to make known the sixfold method of the orthodox tradition; progress toward Bodhi does not fail to proceed by means of this.
My critique is as follows: This passage provides a general explanation of the two characters *fāngbiàn* (expedient means), using them to harmonize the sixfold division of the sutra.
Yet, it remains unclear from what source the term "path of expedient means" (*fāngbiàn dào*) is derived, nor does it capture the intended meaning of the treatise.

The second section, "By knowing the lower," demonstrates the characteristics of the benefit. The intended meaning is as follows: if one does not understand this path, it should be called the Hīnayāna;
it would cause the Buddha-dharma not to abide for long, because the faults have not been exhausted and the two benefits have not been accomplished—thus, it would consist of self-benefit alone.

This meaning becomes even more evident: were it not for this treatise, one would merely call it the Hīnayāna because it dwells only in self-benefit. By means of this treatise, however, it is reversed.

Thereupon, a question was asked: "It may be granted that ordinary persons do not know there are transgressions; but how could it be that a sage does not know this Path and yet gives rise to transgressions?

The answer is: There are two points to consider. First, even sages may still have transgressions. This refers to Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), who, upon entering meditative contemplation (*samāpatti*), are equal to the Buddhas, yet upon emerging from contemplation, are like ordinary persons.
Furthermore, it is only at the second stage (*bhūmi*) that they eliminate erroneous violations of the precepts (*śīla*); therefore, they have not yet entirely escaped [transgression].

"Transcendence" (guò). Second, a sage must know the correct path before they can transcend faults. If one does not know this path, unless they are already a sage, these very faults will obstruct the ground of sagehood;
thus it is called "the sage's transcendence. The first meaning refers to the eradication of faults arising from both ordinary beings and sages.

The second meaning refers to the eradication of faults that cause stagnation among ordinary beings and act as obstructions to sagehood. This is, for example, like the statement that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the obstruction [of ordinary beings].
That which arises is precisely the fault. As for the "obstruction to the knowable" (jñeyāvaraṇa), it is the fault of obstructing the noble ones.

Third, the explanation of the text has two parts. From "This cultivation... onwards, the first part sets forth the headings and divisions. Now, in terms of the three collections (piṭaka), it belongs to the Sūtra Piṭaka;
in terms of the two collections, it belongs to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; and in terms of the various vehicles (yāna), it establishes the Mahāyāna. Regarding these collections and vehicles...
The meaning is fully explained in the *Huayan Dashi*. Question: Who established this? Answer: It was originally established by the Buddha; therefore, it says, "this sūtra," and so forth.

However, the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra), foreseeing that those in the final age would be confused regarding the Buddha’s intent and would claim [the teachings] belong to the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, specifically pointed this out.
If one were to say that the treatise was established previously, then it would pertain to the Master of the Treatise. Furthermore, this sūtra was established...
[The Master] stands [in this position]. Although it is primarily for Bodhisattvas, it also serves the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) because the secondary is subsumed under the primary.

Thus, when it says "that which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas," etc., the commentary explains that it takes the Great and Small Vehicles together from the Jinling assembly, merging them without distinction;

this is not to grasp the Sage’s intent. This [approach] takes the secondary as the primary, which openly contradicts the purport of the treatise. Since this section has already distinguished the seven...

All [the commentaries] state that these are what the Bodhisattvas cultivate; this is the primary intent. The subsequent explanation regarding this bhikṣu further demonstrates that the Mahāyāna shares commonalities with the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha);
this clarifies an inclusive approach rather than the orthodox path. Therefore, in each successive section of the commentary on the sutra, it consistently refers to "Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, if one were to claim that because it is a "Great" [vehicle] that permeates the Small, it is shared with the two vehicles, this would merely be a lower-level distinction made for those of dull faculties.

The preceding selection concerns the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is the teaching common to the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). This is based on a distinction [between them]. What, then, is meant by "conjoined yet undivided"?

Therefore, it is clear that this interpretation greatly deviates from the intent of the treatise. If the *Zhufa ji* (Record of the Abiding Dharma) states: "If one relies on the present sutra, it is originally the Śrāvaka Vehicle."
Regarding the statement in the treatise that "a bodhisattva" has five meanings: first is the intent for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world.
As the sūtra says: "In all that he does, he always acts for one purpose: solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. An objection is raised:

since this treatise still maintains the existence of the three vehicles, how can it be said to have "one purpose"? Furthermore, if this is indeed the fundamental intent, where in the treatise is the second [purpose] shown?
"Is it by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? This gentleman knows only that the Buddha's teachings consist solely of the Great and Small Vehicles;

how could he know that there are many distinctions in the methods of transformation and the rituals of conversion? Second, regarding the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening and unification: the Sūtra says, "That which you all practice is the Bodhisattva path. An objection states:

"The treatise claims that the Mahāyāna is common to the two vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha); this still maintains the three [vehicles]. How can this be considered the unification of the Small [Vehicle]?"
It returns to the Great [Vehicle]. Furthermore, once [the truth] has been revealed and elucidated, all the sūtras of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) can be interpreted according to the Mahāyāna;

why should this treatise alone be the exception? Why would the original intent apply here while other sūtras of the Lesser Vehicle are instead interpreted according to the Lesser Vehicle itself? Third, relying on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* to reapply this intent:

it means that within the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*, the permanence [of the Buddha] was discussed and the nature [of reality] was revealed, thereby resolving doubts regarding provisional teachings. Yet, fearing that after his passing...
Those who cling to the real disparage the provisional; therefore, by emphasizing the partial and the Small Vehicle, one causes those in the future not to give rise to such clinging and disparagement.

Once they have heard that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding, all shall return to the Buddha Vehicle, and all scriptural texts will no longer be partial or small. Thus, those who have left the home life are called true Bodhisattvas and true Śrāvakas.
It was with this intention that the Master of the Treatise propagated and transmitted [the teachings]. An objection is raised: "If it is because he maintains this intention that he now..."

Regarding the Mahāyāna commentators: since all the Śrāvaka-vehicle treatises were composed after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, why do you not preserve this same principle and instead provide a Śrāvaka-style commentary?

Masters such as Vasubandhu were all great Bodhisattvas; how could they have been unaware that after hearing [the teaching on] the permanence [of the Buddha], all scriptural texts would no longer be partial or limited to the Lesser Vehicle, yet still based themselves solely on the intent of the sūtras to provide a Śrāvaka-style commentary? The four flows...

This accords with the intention of responding to the capacities of beings. Since the provisional and limited teachings of the *Hīnayāna* have already been opened and then set aside, the ignorant people of this degenerate age mostly follow them.

If one were to rely upon the *Hīnayāna*, there would certainly be no one to receive and uphold [the teaching]. Therefore, the patriarchs and holy masters of both India and this land all employed the *Mahāyāna* to propagate and praise it;
this deeply accords with the Buddha’s intent and is quite appropriate for the capacities of beings. An objection is raised: "If the *Mahāyāna* is used..."
Regarding those who propagate the "Small" [Vehicle]: they merely cite Mahāyāna meanings briefly within the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna to provide some support for them.

How could there be a single sūtra that is entirely Hīnayāna, or a single treatise that provides entirely Mahāyāna interpretations? Such an example exists neither here in China nor in the Western Regions (India).

This, in turn, causes the masters of these treatises—despite their intention to circulate the teachings in accordance with the capacities of beings—to completely deviate from the intent of the sūtras and to waste their efforts in vain.
[This is] a merit. If one were to cause later generations to imitate this, it would have no connection whatsoever with any of the sutras or treatises.

How could this possibly be the profound intent of the Sage Teacher? It is merely the shallow view of the ignorant. Fifth, regarding the meaning of the mutual inclusion of the Great and the Small Vehicles:

if one relies on the Hinayana, then the Great Vehicle capacity is not included; if one follows the Great Vehicle judgment, then both the Great and Small are included. An objection is raised: if the Great includes the Small...

Therefore, those who judge this to be a Mahāyāna text are entirely mistaken regarding its meaning. For instance, consider the eight sections of the sūtra beginning with "One should know that a person of much desire...

While these passages, when compared to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Eight Great Persons' Awakening*, certainly describe practices cultivated in the Mahāyāna, the commentators [on this text] do not assign it a general title as such, but merely conclude with specific headings. Thus, the interpreters of the sūtra...
This refers to the Hīnayāna; the Master of the Treatise merely designates it by its general name to correspond with the specific titles of the Sūtras.

How could this be an interpretation of the Mahāyāna based exclusively on Hīnayāna practice? It is intended for those of great capacity who harbor small inclinations. There are simply differences in the Sūtras according to the capacities of their respective audiences.
The treatise follows the sūtras in its exposition. How could a great bodhisattva disregard the scriptural text and, acting on private whims, claim that the Great Vehicle subsumes the Small?

From the five points above, it is sufficient to see that the Commentator (Ji-zhu) did not understand the methods of transformation through differentiation or the ritual procedures of transformation; he merely distinguished between the Great and the Small.
Furthermore, his word-by-word commentary on the subsequent sections frequently contradicts the intent of the treatise, as will be seen below. Therefore, all [of these]...

There is no [explicit] citation [of this]. Nevertheless, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) of the Wise Master [Daoxuan], the *Nanshan lüchao* (Nanshan Vinaya Commentary), and the *Xianshou tantian xuanji* (Xianshou’s Exploration of the Profundities) all state that it is a Hīnayāna work (*xiǎoshèng*).

[The *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) notes: "Ancient masters categorized it as a type of Hīnayāna belonging to the 'Beginning and End' section of the *Huàyí mén* (Gate of the Stages of Transformation), such as the *Āgama* and the *Yíjiào jīng* (Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching).

This does not mean they were judging the *Yíjiào jīng* itself as Hīnayāna. Furthermore, after Master Kumārajīva translated this sutra, he immediately included it within the Hīnayāna Piṭaka. Subsequently, during the Chen dynasty, Paramārtha translated this treatise.
In the region of Nan Yue, although it was called Mahāyāna, once the Śāstra Piṭaka had been transmitted through the ages, its sight and hearing were lost.
Consequently, prior to the Kaiyuan era, several catalogues of scriptures, though listing thirty-eight works translated by Paramārtha, contained many that were insufficient for inclusion in the canon.
These treatises were all entered into the "Catalogue of Famous Works with Missing Texts. It was not until the Kaiyuan period that they were [recovered].
The Master [Daoxuan] finally obtained the root text of the treatise; subsequently, based on its doctrinal meaning and the sutra itself, he compiled them both into the Mahāyāna Piṭaka.
Thereafter, various masters, because of this treatise, came to understand that this sutra fully possesses Mahāyāna significance. Thus it was said by the former Zhiyi and Nanshan.
"O Worthy One! Because I had not yet seen the root text of the treatise, I for a time categorized it as belonging to the Hīnayāna.

Later, during the Xingyuan and Zhenyuan eras, the National Teacher Qingliang [Zongmi] finally pointed out in his Great Commentary that the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Buddha's Last Teaching) frequently indicates Mahāyāna meanings.

For instance, in his commentary on the 'Chapter on the Questions of Vidyā' (*Vidyāpraśna-parivarta*), he explains the passage regarding drilling wood to seek fire: 'Before the fire emerges, one repeatedly draws breath. He states that the *Śālistamba-sūtra* corresponds to this by clarifying the 'small water'."
"A constant flow can pierce stone. The *Yanyi* (Exegesis) explains that this refers to the "Eight Awakenings of the Great Men" (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*) and other passages from that same sutra.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on Generating the Resolve" states: "The Bodhisattva attains this vast wisdom; swiftly proceeding toward Bodhi without hindrance, desiring to benefit all sentient beings, he proclaims the Dharma of the Great Man in every place.
The *Shu* (Commentary) explains: "The Dharma of the Great Man refers to the Eight [Awakenings] of the Great Man..."

Regarding "Awakening," the *Chao* (Commentary) explains: "The eight awakenings of the great person are fully elucidated in the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* (as detailed below in the citation). [This is] in the *Shidi-chao* (Commentary on the Ten Stages)."
It is also explained extensively, all of which is reconciled according to the meaning of the Mahāyāna.
By this one may verify that if this treatise had not been translated and hidden in Nan Yue, how could the ancient masters have all considered it to be of the Hīnayāna? Question:

How do we know that the Eight Arousals of a Great Man (*aṣṭau mahāpuruṣavitarkāḥ*) are precisely the Mahāyāna? Answer: As the *Aṣṭamahāpuruṣavitarka-sūtra* states: "These eight matters are indeed [the teachings] of the various..."

This is that which is awakened to by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and great beings; it involves the practice of the path through diligent application and so forth. Furthermore, many predecessors have harbored doubts, asserting that because the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is lacking, this is not the Mahāyāna.

If that were the case, then the Four Noble Truths would belong exclusively to the Śrāvakas, the Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) would be fixed for Pratyekabuddhas, and the Six Perfections would be restricted solely to the Mahāyāna.
Just as in various teachings there are fourfold sets of the Four Truths, how could these be definitively [fixed] for the Pratyekabuddhas?

[Response: Regarding the various Hinayana treatises, it is taught that one cultivates the six perfections separately over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, each reaching its fulfillment at a specific time.

Although these are said to be the practices of a bodhisattva, they still belong to the Hinayana teachings. How can the distinction between Mahayana and Hinayana be determined solely by the [Four] Truths, [Twelve] Conditions, and the [Six] Perfections?
This treatise explains the Four Truths without doubt as being applicable to the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) Four Truths; one should single-mindedly penetrate this to the ultimate degree.
The single-mindedness on the One Meaning, the eight awakenings of the great men, the various gates of samādhi, abiding in the stage of endurance (*kṣānti-bhūmi*),

demonstrating the dharma of non-arising, clarifying the two kinds of selflessness, and realizing the three secret treasuries— all of these fully elucidate the Mahāyāna practice and cultivation of contemplative conduct (*vipaśyanā*).
How could one determine that [the Mahāyāna] is the definitive Great Vehicle merely by contending over whether the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are complete or lacking?
The sevenfold division is as explained in detail below. [Section] One is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the sūtra; second, the commentary’s explanation.

Within this, there are two [sub-sections]. Regarding the first, the commentary states: first is the general and specific classification. As for the term "introductory portion (nidāna) of the sūtra," this refers to the arrangement made by the compilers;
it corresponds to the "specific characteristics" among the three types of sūtra characteristics (1. general characteristics, 2. specific characteristics, 3. abbreviated characteristics). If...

This follows the standard three-part division as explained in the *Gushan Shu*. For example, the *Dashu* (Great Commentary) treats the final two verses of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* as the "Circulation" (*Pravartana*) section;

however, this present treatise differs from that approach. It divides the main body into seven parts (the "Abiding Dharma" and "Proclamation" being included), and since it does not permit a three-part division, it designates the latter six sections as the "Correct Doctrine" (*Saddharma*).

In that case, the three divisions would not be established, and the seven divisions would again be conflated (thus losing both of Aśvaghoṣa’s and Tiantai’s two intended meanings). As for "benefit," there is nothing in the Buddha’s appearance in the world that is not beneficial.
Now, by manifesting the initial turning [of the wheel] and the subsequent teachings, this benefit is made complete; therefore, it is said that he "achieves the ultimate.

This, then, refers to the "Initiation" section within the two types of prefaces; while its text contains the "Certification and Faith," the six elements are not fully present here, as this section contains only...

Since the Master was presiding over the assembly at that time, and as the text already contains this implication, it is not necessary to provide a full correspondence. To do so would be mere forced interpretation (as in the two commentaries).

[For example,] they take the "brief exposition of the essentials of the Dharma" as the fulfillment of faith, and because Ānanda’s compilation must have been heard directly from the Buddha, they take this as the fulfillment of hearing. However, this is a hollow correspondence; neither the hearing nor the faith is established. Why? Because in both cases, the fulfillment of faith is not realized.

If one takes "evam" (thus) as a term signifying conformity to faith, this does not refer to the specific Dharma being expounded below. Now, since the essentials of the Dharma expounded below are taken as the fulfillment of faith, this constitutes a combined explanation of "evam mayā śrutam" (Thus have I heard), wherein "evam" is used to point toward the Dharma.

These words do not constitute the fulfillment of the "Preamble of Authenticity" (*saddharma-āptāgama*). Therefore, those who engage in such forced interpretations are entirely ignorant of the structural conventions of scriptural commentaries. However, it is not necessarily the case that all sutras possess these six elements of the preamble;

for instance, the *Ullambana Sūtra* contains only five. In its enumeration of the assembly, it mentions only Maudgalyāyana alone, which immediately places it within the "Introductory Section on the Occasion" (*nidāna*).

Furthermore, since the phrase "having heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) appears prior to the section on faith, we know that this is not unique to this sutra, even though it is a testament left at the time of death.
The circumstances were unusual (as in the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, where the assembly is likewise not enumerated).
Second, the detailed explanation according to specific divisions has six parts. First, the Dharma Master’s accomplishment of ultimate merit.

Second, the general indication at the beginning of the treatise. Regarding the first, the general characteristics: it is "general" for two reasons, namely the two meanings found in the subsequent detailed explanation. First:

The first is the general [classification] because of the merits of all Buddhas. The second is the general [classification] because of the purity of their own essence; since this purity of essence also applies universally to all, it is considered general.

Regarding the two specific characteristics, they likewise correspond to the latter two meanings: first, specifically regarding merit, he is called Śākyamuni (the Benevolent One) because he skillfully brings forth sentient beings;
second, specifically regarding lineage, he is called Śākya because his family and clan are noble. Third is the general and the specific.

Regarding "the epithet" (*xiàng*): it refers to the two meanings—general and specific—each of which applies to the Buddha. Second, because the [epithets] are assigned to the three bodies (*trikāya*), one obtains merit by addressing him as such.
As for the case of Maitreya, he was named solely based on his clan lineage. Furthermore, regarding the names of various Buddhas, they do not necessarily possess all three bodies;
would it then follow that there is no merit in addressing them? If the word "Buddha" is assigned to the three bodies, this is self-evident and requires no further explanation.

The treatise provides a detailed explanation of the middle and lower [categories]. Regarding Śākyamuni: "Śākya" is translated here as "Capable One" (*Nengren*) and also as "Straight Forest" (*Zhilín*). The old translations rendered it as "Crossing the Wujiao.
"Capable One" (*Nengren*) refers to his virtue; "Straight Forest" (*Zhilín*) refers to his location. The old translations used only the meaning of "Capable" (*Neng*).

The old translations also called him "Śākyamuni. The *Ruiying jing* states: "Śākya means 'Capable' (*Neng*), and Muni means 'Sage' (*Ru*. Now, based on his transformative birth, he is designated as "Benevolent" (*Ren*) due to his skillful means.

This refers to his ability. Furthermore, "Śākya" denotes the preeminence of his clan, while "Gautama" denotes the preeminence of his lineage. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Śākyamuni belongs to the Gautama clan.
When it is now said that he is of the "family and clan," this does not refer to Gautama; rather, it cites Śākya alone, which likewise signifies the preeminence of his lineage.
This is because, from the beginning of the kalpa, they have been passed down through generations as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*). "Gautama" means "earth."
"Lord" (*bhūpati*) refers to the successive lords of the land. From antiquity until King Susīma, all were Cakravartin kings.
From King Ajita-mahādeva there were four sons: first, Mukhacandra; second, Gajaprabha; third, Mārgadarśin; and fourth, Alaṃkāra.

These four sons were suspected [of treason] and were banished to the north of the Snowy Mountains, into the forest of *ṛju-vṛkṣa*. The people delighted in their transformative influence, and they flourished into a powerful state.
In his native land, the father king sighed, saying, "My son possesses such capability," and thus established his clan name (śagotra). Therefore, it is known that his ancient clan was Gautama;

later, when he moved to Veṇuvana, he formally designated his lineage, and thus it became a renowned clan. A "clan name" (śagotra) is like the names Cui or Lu; a "lineage" (kula) refers to the ancestral line.
As with the Bo-ling clan and others, because he was a Śākya of the Gautama lineage, it is said that his family surname was noble.

The *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states that when the Bodhisattva was about to descend to be born, he first contemplated five matters of causal conditions; the fourth is said to be the contemplation of various clans.
What is most flourishing? Among all lineages, the Śākyas are foremost; they are the descendants of Ikṣvāku and the progeny of the noble kings.
These two records refer to the four castes (*varṇa*) of Western India. The Śākyas belong to the royal lineage, that is, the Kṣatriya caste; therefore, they are called "noble and honorable.
If this is so, then all who are of the Kṣatriya caste are noble and honorable. Why then is it said to apply to the Śākyas alone? This...
This is a general name, not the specific characteristic intended here. Furthermore, in the listing of the castes, the Kṣatriya is placed first among the four;
this is merely forcing the second to be the first in order to conform to one's own views. However, among the four castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the foremost.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent lineage; the Kṣatriya and others are inferior."
Regarding the castes (such as Vaiśyas and Śūdras), non-Buddhists maintain that because Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā, they are the most superior.

Furthermore, they cite the appearance of various Buddhas in the world: if a person values virtuous conduct, they are born into the Brahmin caste (as was the case with Kāśyapa Buddha, who belonged to the Kāśyapa clan, which is a Brahmin caste). However, since the present Śākyamuni belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, he is the one who is noble.
Is it because the family lineage of the Brahmin household is considered base that [the Buddha] is contrasted with other Buddhas?

One must not fail to realize that these arise merely according to the inclinations and preferences of people's capacities; it is not that the four castes are inherently noble or base by their very form.

Now, the Master of the Treatise specifically refers to those who have been Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin) for successive generations—namely, the Śākyas of the Gautama clan—and thus speaks of their "noble and honorable family lineage. As for the term "Muni":
The *Past Causes and Effects Sūtra* (*Pubbsaṃyuktakāraṇasūtra*) states: "Muni" refers to the fulfillment of the merits of body, speech, and mind.
This is said to be the merit of all Buddhas, specifically because the merits of the three vehicles of all Buddhas are fully perfected.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Yojanas* states: "Muni" means "capable of pacifying," and is also called "non-discrimination"; this is the principle (*tattva*).

The essence of wisdom is entirely pure (the old commentary translates this as "quiescent silence," which is a forced interpretation of the treatise). The character for "Buddha" is easy to understand and thus not explained separately;
it possesses the four meanings mentioned above, comprising both general and specific characteristics. If one were to explain the word "Buddha," its meaning would be as commonly taught.

The second merit has three parts. In the section "Opening the Dharma" below, first is the topical statement: because the Deer Park is the place where the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, it is the site of the initial bestowal of the Way;
therefore, it is called a *bodhimaṇḍa* (place of the Way). (Both commentaries claim it is the place of attaining enlightenment, which is incorrect. The rest may be understood.
Regarding the section "Discourse on these two below," there are two parts that demonstrate the meaning.

As for the phrase "to manifest and explain the meaning of 'turning' (*vartana*)," this refers to the initial turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths (the demonstration of characteristics, the exhortation to practice, and the realization of the fruit, as is customary). Therefore, it is called "turning. Because it occurred at the very beginning, it carries the sense of "successive turning" (*parāvṛtti*);

thus, the final [turning] lacks this quality and is simply called "explaining" (*deśanā*). Nevertheless, "turning" also carries the sense of "explaining," while there are instances where "explaining" does not carry the sense of "turning. This...

This demonstrates that the initial and final meanings differ. Thus, although the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) are all termed "wheels of Dharma," the term is used specifically for the first.
