(To gather various flowers. Just as one obtains good or bad food,) one takes only their flavor; this metaphor signifies that by engaging with phenomena, one takes up the flavor of equanimity to sustain the Dharma-body.

"Not damaging color and fragrance" is a metaphor for not giving rise to increase or decrease. Since one does not give rise to increase or decrease, the mind’s impartial contemplation of phenomena (*dharmas*) is accomplished.
Therefore, it is further stated: "It is a manifestation, not a contemplation that destroys phenomena. The *Zhufa* (Abiding in the Dharma) says:

"The *Nanshan Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts of the Southern Mountain), in its explanation of the verses on the abbreviated teaching, states: 'Not damaging color and fragrance' is a metaphor for not excessively seeking [to change] things so as to destroy the faith of worldly people; this is identical to the present [case]."

They are not the same; there is no need for further reconciliation. Now, it is said that [the commentator] correctly takes the present sutra’s statement, "One should not seek much, lest one destroy one's wholesome mind," as the basis for explaining that verse;
thus he says so. However, the subsequent sutra passage is not actually joined with the preceding one.
Furthermore, because the original treatise was long hidden and ancient masters had not seen it, this explanation was made. If one were to reconcile that verse with the present treatise:

Although the basis of the analogy is the same, the substance of the analogy differs slightly. If one observes without impairing the phenomena (*dharma*), it is also the same as the present case. That verse says:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, neither destroying its color nor its fragrance, but taking only its nectar and departing; so too does a bhikṣu enter a village.
He does not oppose the affairs of others, nor does he observe what is done or left undone; he observes only his own mental conduct, whether it be correct or not."
This is correct. One enters the assembly to gather flowers; by not contravening others, one performs the act of non-action.

This corresponds to [the previous section], which concerned others, whereas the present section concerns oneself. By observing one’s own bodily conduct, one attains the flavor; this accords with the intent of the present treatise.

For if one observes the affairs of others, it impairs their color and fragrance, and thus one loses their flavor. Not impairing the affairs of others is intended so that one may achieve self-observation.
This is the Dharma. As the verse says: "One should simply observe one's own bodily conduct. This does not refer to damaging the faith of others;

rather, it refers to the fact that such [conduct] would successively destroy one's own wholesome mind. Therefore, this interpretation was made. Judging by the present treatise, it seems that [the previous view] has lost its essential meaning.

Fifth, regarding the accomplishment of the merit of not receiving sustenance in vain: since receiving [food] is for the purpose of removing affliction, how could one need excessive eating that would damage the work of the Path? Thus...

It is not for nothing that you receive this; it also applies to two aspects. First, by means of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), one removes hunger and thirst to treat the suffering of the physical body and thereby accomplish the work of the Path.
Second, by not giving rise to the mental karma of greed and so forth, one extinguishes and eliminates the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As cited from the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* by Saṃgharakṣa: "It is just as when many birds are captured and hidden in a large vessel; they are inspected at the proper times and fed with nourishment at the proper times."
As their feathers and tails grew long, they were trimmed and clipped from time to time; those that were plump were selected for daily provision in the kitchen.
Among them was one bird who reflected within herself: "If I eat much, I shall become so fat that I will die; yet if I starve and do not eat, I shall likewise lose my life."
"One should examine oneself and eat sparingly; greed harms the skin, while moderation makes the fur and feathers glossy. One should emerge from the cage according to one's intention.
Thereupon, he ate sparingly, his fur and feathers became glossy, and he was able to act as he pleased. It is the same for that practitioner of the path:
he examines himself within, thinking, "If I eat too much, I will become dazed and unable to cultivate the Way, nor attain contemplation."

Only wholesome dharmas [flourish], while unwholesome dharmas increase greatly; all this is due to eating too much, which prevents one from attaining Buddhahood. A sūtra states that there are five afflictions:
first, frequent defecation; second, frequent urination; third, excessive sleepiness; fourth, physical heaviness that renders one incapable of practicing the Path;
and fifth, many ailments resulting from undigested food. One who knows the proper time achieves merit; one who seeks excessively does not.
Because of [knowing] the time, the wholesome mind is not impaired. Regarding the many mental factors (*caitta-dharma*): if one eats much, the mind will frequently give rise to further seeking;
therefore, the samādhi of eating little cannot manifest before one. Only by knowing the time and seeking this merit can one accomplish the samādhi of eating little.
Although the treatise clarifies the samādhi of eating little, it does so in terms of the food of the mind and its mental factors.

The "wise" (vidvān) verify and know that the teaching regarding the practice of eating little—that is, the *alpa-āhāra-samādhi*—is situated below the section on "various kinds of food" (*nānā-āhāra*); this clearly demonstrates its incorrectness.
As for the statement regarding "calculating during the preparatory stage" (*upāya-kāla*), it refers to weighing the amount of strength a bull can bear;
just as in the parable one calculates whether the bull's strength is sufficient, so too in the Dharma one contemplates how much food and drink is appropriate to consume.
This refers to the method and the appropriate means for knowing [the signs]. Regarding the statement "corresponding to the method of accomplishment" (*sādhana-yoga*):
it means that the scripture does not permit one to exceed the proper measure by exhausting one's strength. One should employ the effort according to the capacity of an ox’s strength;

if one does not exceed the ox's capacity, its strength will not be exhausted, and thus one knows the time of accomplishment. Therefore, it is called "corresponding. As for the statement "showing the fault of eating too much": [it follows that one must avoid excess].
In the analogy, one does not employ the strength of an ox; regarding the practice of moderation, one does not eat excessively.

For this reason, it is called "eating little. Among the six aforementioned virtues, the first is named "receiving food like medicine," and the fifth is "receiving it for the sake of removing affliction."
Sixth, because one does not seek much, one achieves the Samādhi of Eating Little. Second, it clarifies the mind of the contemplation of equality.

Third, when the contemplation is perfected, the principle manifests. Fourth, by means of an analogy, these are combined to reveal the ultimate mind (paramārtha-citta) and achieve the Samādhi of Non-Eating.

Third, the antidote to the suffering of indolence and sleep, in two parts. Having already explained the former [the antidote to overeating], this follows next because the former treats that which gives rise [to indolence and sleep], while this treats that which is given rise to. Second, the explanation based on the heading, in two parts:

first, citing the sūtra; second, the commentary’s explanation, in two parts. Regarding the commentary’s section beginning with "The treatise says," the first shows the antidote: "without weariness" refers to the following.
Vigor and reflection. That is to say, one subsequently reflects and observes; both serve to remedy indolence and sleepiness. Second, the two factors to be remedied are clarified.

In this treatise, the middle and lower sections first discuss indolence and sleepiness together to clarify their intended meaning. First, there are two points regarding the inquiry. First, the question asks:
"Since the two states of indolence and sleepiness differ in that the former pertains to the mind and the latter to the body, why are they discussed together? Second, the question [continues].
Question: Since the two factors of *kausīdya* (indolence) and *middha* (sleepiness) each have their own distinct essence, why are they spoken of together?

For *kausīdya* has the nature of laziness (*ālasya*), while *middha* has the nature of mental obscurity and contraction (*līnatva*). Since the essences of body and mind are different, they should each function as a distinct hindrance;

this is the intent of the present inquiry. Regarding the explanation that follows, there are two interpretations. As for the first point regarding the nature of body and mind: because they are mutually dependent, it is said—
Because the mind is indolent, the body becomes weary and heavy; because the body is weary and heavy, the mind becomes indolent.

Therefore, it is said that these two are mutually concordant, meaning they accord with one another and thus constitute a single affliction. Second, because these two are mentioned together among the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), they are likewise spoken of together here as obstacles.

As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Buddha taught the five hindrances: first, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*); second, ill-will (*vyāpāda*); third, lethargy and drowsiness (*styānamiddha*)."

Regarding the five hindrances—namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt—the commentary asks:

"For what reason are sloth and torpor, as well as restlessness and remorse, each established as a single hindrance despite having distinct natures? It replies: "Because their nutriment, antidote, and function are identical, they are each established as one.

"Nutriment" refers to that which is consumed; it is also called "provision. "Antidote" refers to that which counteracts; it is also called "non-nutriment. "Function" refers to their activity; it is also called "efficacy. Based on this, [the two pairs are combined] due to their respective states of mental dullness...
Although torpor and sleep are two, their nutriment and non-nutriment are the same. What is called the nutriment of the hindrance of torpor and sleep?
It consists of five factors: first, drowsiness; second, lack of joy; third, yawning; fourth, irregularity of diet; and fifth, dullness and inferiority of mind.
What is called the non-nutriment of this hindrance? It is the perception of light. The functional application of these two is also the same; that is, both are able to...

[The above is all from the treatise. Evaluation: Since, among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), torpor and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) are combined into a single hindrance, and since it is now stated that they are spoken of together as being among the five kinds of obstacles to concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*), the term "obstacles to concentration" is used. Furthermore, the treatise states:

"In the realms of form and formlessness, there are no unwholesome states; however, because these five [hindrances] are unwholesome, they exist only in the desire realm. This is based on these five hindrances.

It exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and directly obstructs the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the two higher realms. This is because it is defined here according to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

Regarding the categories of torpor (*middha*) and lethargy (*styāna*), their essential natures are not distinct. However, when the Abhidharma of the Hīnayāna defines their essential substance, there is a distinction between torpor and lethargy;

yet, when the Dharma is expounded, both are listed as the fourth hindrance and termed the "hindrance of sleep" (*middha-nīvaraṇa*). This is because within the state of sleep, there is no separate entity that is lethargy. Thus it is known.

This is explained together. If one interprets it as cited above, one will certainly see its erroneous understanding. Second, regarding the explanation of the text by taking "sleep" (*svapna*) to imply "indolence" (*ālasya*), there are two parts within the treatise.
First, the distinction is established based on conditions: since Arhats who possess a remaining body may still reside in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because the mind is pure, although one does not fall into torpor or sleep due to the state of the mind itself, one may still fall asleep due to food or the time of day.

There are two reasons for this, as explained below: first, because both the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi*) and the afflictions of conduct (*bhāvanā-heya*) have been severed, torpor does not arise from the mind;

second, there are no hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which implies the absence of a defiled mind. However, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it does not even exist in the higher realms.

If even the afflictions of the higher realms—which are defiled by views and discursive thought—cannot act as an obscuration, how much less could the afflictions of the lower realms? Thus, there is nothing that can obscure them.

By contrast, this reveals that sentient beings in the desire realm do indeed possess obscurations; therefore, sleep arises from the mind, and all [beings] therein possess these three [characteristics].
Second, regarding the two [types of] antidotes corresponding to the headings: the treatise states, "The three below," etc. First, these combined antidotes address the preceding two.
If sleep arises from the mind, one who possesses meditative observation and wisdom can immediately subdue it. However, if it arises due to eating, even Arhats cannot entirely avoid it;
thus, it cannot be suppressed without diligence. Therefore, the first two are categorized as being addressed by diligence alone.

This is the treatment. The first two phrases explain the passage from "during the day" down to "regulating the breath. The statement that [afflictions] have not been severed since beginningless time refers specifically to the hindrance of sleep;
therefore, one should apply oneself with diligence. In the sutra, "wholesome dharmas" refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth.

Since those practicing meditation in the desire realm may fear the arising of thoughts of sleep when the proper time arrives, they use reciting the sutras as their regulation. "Regulation" (or "rest") means...

"Breath" refers to the breath of sleep; therefore, one uses the recitation of sutras to dispel it. Furthermore, the passage below—"Do not sleep," and so forth—is cited because those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) attained their fruits while in a manifest body.
Now, by citing them, it is said that one must not let a single lifetime pass in vain, but should instead attain the realization of a fruit.
"Abiding in the Dharma" refers to the fact that the teachings of the Noble Path reside within the Two [Vehicles].

The *Śāstra* explains that this applies to both the Buddha-vehicle and the Bodhisattva-path. How could it be that the *Śāstra* restricts the Buddha-vehicle to the Mahāyāna alone, while suggesting that the Hīnayāna attains [enlightenment] in a single lifetime?
Furthermore, how could the Sūtra be definitively restricted to the Two Vehicles? It is simply because the Mahāyāna employs skillful means to guide and receive those of inferior capacity.
This also represents a dual confusion regarding both the Sūtras and the Śāstras.
Regarding the two specific remedies for the latter two [hindrances], the Śāstra states "the rest below," which first provides a general indication.

The subsequent Sūtra text clarifies that the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and so forth all remedy sleep arising from the mind; however, the previous mention of "diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas" also implicitly includes contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*). The following section clarifies...
Regarding the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*): it is not that diligence is unnecessary for its extensive analysis;

therefore, two remedies are distinguished. These two are explained separately. First, concerning the middling and inferior [faculties]: first, the heading; second, the explanation, which has two parts. First, the remedy consisting of reflection and investigation (*cintā-vipaśyanā-pratipakṣa*).

Second. The first is the inferior [method]. Initially, one contemplates the impermanence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). First, one contemplates the arising, ceasing, and disintegration of the five aggregates.
As the Sūtra says, "The fire of impermanence" refers precisely to the contemplation of all that arises and ceases. "It burns all worlds" refers to the destruction of the aggregates.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three kinds of worlds: first, the world of the five aggregates; second, the world of sentient beings; and third, the world of the physical realm. Now...
It is foremost because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are not one; thus they are called "all" (*sarva*). Regarding the term "world" (*loka*), there are two meanings:
first, the sense of concealment, for it conceals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); second, the sense of being destructible, for it is transmuted by the three periods of time.

Furthermore, "intermediate" (*antara*) refers to falling into the midst of falsehood; since the world itself is this intermediate state, it is named "the world" (*loka*). Now, [the term] encompasses both of these two meanings. And...

All [phenomena] are observed as being subject to destruction. Furthermore, it is shown below: "Since one contemplates impermanence, one should early seek deliverance and not allow the mind to run wild by giving rise to sleep.
The meaning is this: if one does not contemplate impermanence and allows sleep to arise from the mind, then meditative concentration and wisdom will not manifest;

one will remain perpetually in the lower realms and be unable to deliver oneself from the three realms. Furthermore, it is shown below that the three contemplations [perceive] the aggregates and so forth as permanent.

Regarding "harmful" (*ghāta*): the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) are also called "spheres" (*sthāna*). As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Accumulation, the gate of arising, and lineage—these are the meanings of aggregate, element, and base.

This is because a sense of shame (*hrī*) is foremost among all adornments. That other stages are free from fault means that the hook of shame restrains people from what is not the Dharma (*adharma*).

While in various sūtras and śāstras the characteristics of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are distinguished, the quality of "embarrassment" (*lajjā*) is common to both; in this treatise, "shame" (*hrī*) is thus used to encompass both.
This is the meaning. Therefore, the explanation that one’s own ground is adorned while other grounds are faultless applies generally to the meaning of *hrī* (shame).
Specifically, however, "self" refers to *hrī*, while "other" refers to *apatrāpya* (embarrassment). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One who has *hrī* does not commit evil themselves;

one who has *apatrāpya* does not incite others to do so. One who has *hrī* feels internal shame; one who has *apatrāpya* discloses [their faults] to others. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 44, also says:
The sense of shame arising from within is *hrī* (self-respect); the sense of shame arising from without is *apatrāpya* (dread of blame). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, fascicle six, states:

"Self-respect (*hrī*) has as its nature the honoring and revering of the worthy and the good by relying on the power of oneself and the Dharma; its function is to counteract the lack of self-respect and to cease unwholesome conduct."
*Hrī* (shame) relies on worldly power; its nature is to slight and reject violence and evil. Its function is to counteract *anapatrāpya* (lack of shame) and to bring an end to unwholesome conduct.
The distinctions between *hrī* and *apatrāpya* cited above are all made by dividing them according to self and others.

While *lajjā* (modesty/shamefulness) applies to both, although this treatise maintains the distinction between self and others, its meaning seems to encompass both *hrī* and *apatrāpya*. Yet, the Sūtra speaks only of "the clothing of *hrī* and *apatrāpya*. As for *hrī*:

The iron hook. It is verified that in the Sūtras, shame (*hrī*) subsumes modesty (*apatrāpya*). However, from the perspective of one's own ground, it is like clothing, for one adorns oneself with the shame of pure precepts.
From the perspective of another's ground, shame is like a hook, for through the shame of pure precepts, one causes others to feel awe and respect.

Second, the two types of phenomena that are mutually contradictory regarding the mundane and supramundane. The treatise further demonstrates this below. First, regarding mundane merit: this refers to "self-restraint" as mentioned in the Sūtra.
Although one lacks supramundane pure dharmas, one nonetheless practices self-restraint and thereby accomplishes mundane merit.

If one were to give rise to anger, it might still be excusable; for laypeople in the world are permitted to experience desire, which constitutes both favorable and adverse conditions. Since this is so...

Because it contradicts the enjoyment of a layperson (*avadātavasana*)—where "contradiction" means contradicting one's inclinations and "conformity" means conforming to them; this contradiction or conformity of desires is termed the meaning of "enjoyment" (similarly, as with the four types of minds previously mentioned, offerings are termed "enjoyment," and enjoyment is also defined in relation to the mind)—when an adverse object appears before one, if one cannot suppress or endure it and instead gives rein to the arising of anger, this does not yet constitute a violation of principle.
Therefore, it is said that there is no ultimate contradiction. Second, regarding the supramundane path, the treatise next demonstrates the first method below.

Regarding the phrase "among the two types of phenomena experienced in the world," this refers to the aforementioned layperson who experiences these two phenomena through both opposition and compliance.
While previously there was not yet absolute opposition, here there is total opposition. As for the remaining two metaphors below, Guo Pu said:
"The sudden and violent discharge of thunder is called a *pīlì* (thunderclap). The *Zhuangzi* states: "There is fire within water; it can thus consume the great mass [of the earth]."

This is the "Thunderbolt Fire. Second, it treats the obstacle of arrogance (*māna*). First, the heading is presented: whereas the preceding anger generally obstructs the noble path for both oneself and others, the present arrogance specifically obstructs one’s own noble path;
therefore, it follows next. Second, the scripture is cited. Third, the commentary explains these two points. First, the subject and object are clarified.

"Treating two [points]. The commentary says, 'Below'... This first section provides a general indication. The first phrase identifies the obstacle and its remedy. "Manifesting below" indicates the remedial factor (*pratipakṣa*):

because one possesses a sense of self-importance, one treats others with contempt; thus, the absence of such a sense of self-importance constitutes the practice. "Remaining far removed from arrogance" is that which is to be treated (the obstacle).
The Sūtra speaks of "pride" (*māna*), which is explained here as "arrogance" (*unnati*). This is because both are forms of arrogance. Because...
This is a general overview of the specific categories. Regarding the specific meanings, there are two distinct senses. "The hundred dharmas" refers as follows:

*mada* (intoxication/arrogance) is the nature of generating defiled attachment toward one's own flourishing prosperity; it is a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*). *Māna* (pride) is the nature of exalting oneself over others by relying on one's own qualities;

it is a root affliction (*mūlakleśa*). The *Abhidharmakośa* also states: "Pride arises in relation to another's mind, whereas intoxication arises from being stained by one's own nature. Herein, the subtle [distinctions] are treated.

Therefore, the commentary on the Sūtra explains "swift extinction" as being due to the distancing of even subtle arisings. If that which is subtle is already treated, it can be known that the coarse is likewise addressed.
There are two reasons why this obstacle is treated in the second stage: first, because one is prone to transgressing; second, because it is a profound obstacle.

Because pride (*māna*) consists of seven and nine types, it is common to both what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The seven and nine [types of] pride arise from three;

all are common to what is abandoned by seeing and cultivation. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Great Collection) is likewise [in agreement]. (That is to say, the nine prides arise from three prides: namely, first, pride (*māna*); second, over-pride (*atimāna*); and third, the pride of thinking oneself inferior (*ūnamāna*). Regarding these seven and nine prides, their names and meanings are as explained elsewhere.

Furthermore, because the pride of self (*asmimāna*) and the four afflictions within consciousness equally obstruct the Noble Path due to their profound nature, this is distinguished [as a separate category].

This treats arrogance (*māna*). Since it is called "haughtiness" (*unnati*) equally in relation to oneself and others, the seven phrases are assigned separately to the [categories of] superior and inferior; in all cases, one acts with physical and mental conduct that despises [others], thereby departing from haughtiness.

Thus, it is said there are "seven phrases of practice for distancing [oneself]. Regarding the first: because the head is honored as supreme and the crown of the head is the highest of all, it is so called.
Superior, superior. Furthermore, because shaving [the head] comes first, it is called "first breaking" [the adornments]. Regarding the second point, "other places":

this does not merely refer to removing the hair and discarding the ornaments of crowns and tiaras; it also refers to the body universally discarding other fine things such as the jade and gems one wears.

The *Yuzao* (The Adornment of Jade) says: "In antiquity, the gentleman invariably wore jade. Only during mourning did he not do so. Unless there was a specific reason, the gentleman never removed the jade from his person."
Therefore, all such [colors] are now abandoned. Among the three [types of robes], one wears those made of the five primary colors or intermediate colors for the sake of a virtuous mind;
monastics differ from this, and thus they wear robes of dyed (ruined) color. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One must not keep robes dyed with superior colors."

When [a robe] is to be ruined [for use], it should be dyed the color of a *kāṣāya* (here translated as "improper color" or "dyed color"). It is also said that when one obtains a new garment, one must apply three types of dyed ruinous colors:

blue (*nīla*), black (*kṛṣṇa*), and madder-brown (*māñjiṣṭha*). The *Vinaya-śīlōpadeśa* states: "Blue refers to copper-green; black refers to various muds and the like; madder-brown refers to the juices of various trees.

(Regarding the translation of the *Vinaya*: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was translated in the Wu region of the north; because it was not seen there, they used the madder-brown dyeing method. I [Nanshan...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Vinaya, likely by Daoxuan of Nanshan.*
I myself have personally seen the bark of the *múlán* tree in the capital of Shu; it is a brilliant dark red-black and can be used for dyeing.
It has a faint fragrance, and there are also those who use it as incense. If one refers to the *Jìguī zhuàn*, it states that all monastic robes may be dyed *gāndhāra*.
This may be done using powdered *dìhuáng* (turmeric), or the yellow of *jīngbiè* (barberry), and so forth; these are all suitable to be dyed with red.
The soil is red ochre, or perhaps the earth of the crabapple tree is purple; once dyed, it remains so until the garment is worn through—so why seek anything else?
Furthermore, the "wrinkled mulberry" green border is precisely what is prohibited by the regulations. True purple-brown is not worn in the West.

Some cite the *Śrī-guṇaratna-saṃyukta-sūtra* (or *Yizu jing*), which prescribes distinct colors for the five classes of robes. That sutra states: "When the Buddha was in the world, the assembly of monks wore only the garments of the deceased."

Regarding miscellaneous robes: once, when Rājagṛha was practicing alms-rounds, he returned empty-handed. The Buddha, knowing his past conduct, instructed the assembly of monks to divide the Vinaya into five sections and to have five types of robe colors, so that each might follow the practices of one specific school. Consequently, a regulation was established. Why?

Because each school was named after its own particular excellence, and the colors of their robes were designated accordingly. The Dharmaguptaka school excelled in penetrating the flavor of principle and in guiding and benefiting sentient beings.
Those of the Sarvāstivāda school, who are widely learned, quick-witted, and proficient, and who guide others through the transformation of the Dharma, should wear robes of red color.

Those of the Kāśyapīya school, who are diligent, courageous, and swift, and who gather in and protect sentient beings, should wear robes of dark (soaked-in-ink) color. Those of the Mahīśāsaka school, who are energetic and resolute, and who lead the way for all beings, should wear robes of madder-brown color.
The Mahīśāsaka school contemplates the subtle and penetrates the profound and mysterious; they should wear blue robes.

The Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studies the various sūtras and expounds upon their principles and meanings; they should wear yellow robes. From that time onward, they were permitted to receive abundant food.

Thus, even during the Buddha’s lifetime, the five schools were already distinguished by the colors of their robes. If one refers to the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the *Fahua Xuanyi*), it says: "The [remaining]..."

The *Śāsanāntima-samādhi-sūtra* exists in five recensions; these are distinct from the five recensions [of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*] that appeared after the Buddha’s passing, though they share the same title.
The supplementary note states: "If one relies on the original sūtras, the titles are identical in all cases; it is not known why this is so. Furthermore, the *Vinaya-piṭaka-śāstra* (Lüchāo) states:

"Regarding the five-colored [manuscripts] among the *Śāsanāntima-vinaya-sūtra*, these are not part of the authentic canon. Those who lack knowledge employ them" (this point remains undetermined as to its accuracy even today). Nevertheless, the above has clarified [the matter].
Regarding the color of robes, as for the actual material used for the robe's substance: on Mount Nan-shan (Nanshan), cloth is exclusively used as the primary substance.

Thus, the *Lüchao* (Exegesis on the Vinaya) explains the precept concerning bedding made from wild silkworm silk, stating: "According to the *Sifen* [Vinaya], making a new bedding out of mixed wild silkworm silk constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The *Sifen* [Vinaya] records that because a bhikṣu went to a silkworm-raising household and begged for both raw silk and processed silk to make bedding, he waited there.
Seeing them making noise while working with raw silk cocoons, he rebuked and regulated them:

"Whether they work with pure [silk], or mix it with *kṣauma* (linen), wool, hemp, or other fibers, if they produce anything by mixing these together, each shall be finely chopped and hacked with axes and hatchets, then mixed with mud to plaster walls or mounds.
(The upper part of this passage is abbreviated; the following is quoted in full). In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, "kauśeya" is a name for cotton; it is like the raising of silkworms in the land of Qin.

Regarding the Dharma: to beg for silk cocoons, cotton thread, or cloth to make robes constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. As for "requisites" (*śayanāsana*), these refer to the three robes (the tri-cīvara);

that is, the collective name for the three robes is "requisites," just as in this land [of China] they are designated by their general term. In foreign lands, there are generally two ways of making robes: first, by finely splitting cloth into strips and weaving them like felt;
second, by spinning cotton into thread and weaving it into cloth. These are also used to constitute the three robes for wearing.

Because it was obtained through begging, its creation constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Even if mixed with a single hair, one commits an offense. Regarding *kauśeya*:

this refers to the finest part of silk, the thread that first emerges from the mouth of a silkworm. In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it says: "Leather sandals and shoes, *kauśeya* garments—such clothing as these must not be kept at all.
This is the correct teaching of the Sūtras and Vinayas. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When offered by a silkworm-keeper..."
Cotton: Having received it, one should give it to the Saṃgha and must not use it oneself. By comparing these various sections, we know that the intent behind the prohibition is grave.

If even wild silk constitutes an offense, how much more so domestic silk? If even mixed silk constitutes an offense, how much more so pure [silk]? There are many who beg for materials to make the three robes;
these must be cut up and discarded (*cīvara-pratyādeśana*), and they are not permitted to be kept or worn. To wear them is an offense. Furthermore, it says:

The four precepts concerning black-fur bedding and so forth are collectively designated as the "three robes" (*tricīvara*). This has been a point of doubt for people since antiquity that remains unresolved to this day.

[The passage beginning with] "The *saṃghāṭī* made of felt according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, up to 'requisites for life'" (the above are excerpts from the *Vinaya-śāstra*) is precisely what the Tripitaka Master Yijing refutes in his *Nanhai Jiguigui Neifa Zhuan*.
The *Zhuan* states: "In general, when discussing silk and woven fabrics, these are indeed permitted by the Sage."
Why do you so strenuously obstruct [this]? It is merely a matter of establishing a formal rule to sever [the practice]. This is because one wishes to avoid the proliferation of complications.
Since both the five schools and the four divisions [of the Vinaya] in the Five Indies all employ [these materials], how can one discard easily obtained silk and seek difficult-to-obtain fine cloth?

Is there anything that more utterly hinders the Path than this? This is precisely what is meant by "not enforcing what is not a regulation. Consequently, those who are fond of novelty and uphold the Vinaya...

Those who do so increase their own arrogance and look down upon others; they are not guests who seek to diminish their desires. Internally they give rise to shamelessness, while externally they harbor malice.

This is truly an obstruction to the long path [of liberation]. What more need be said? If one were to personally beg for cocoons and witness with one's own eyes the harm done to the insects, this would be something even a worldly person should not practice, let alone one whose heart aspires to transcendence. To cite such things as proof is profoundly [misguided].
This cannot yet be finalized. If there is a donor who brings [the cloth] with a pure intention, one must immediately chant "rejoicing" (*anumodana*) to accept it.
Using it to sustain the body and cultivate virtue is beyond reproach. Regarding the dharma-robes of the Five Regions (India): they may be embroidered or sewn as one pleases;

the threads of the fabric need not be distinguished by their orientation (lengthwise or crosswise). In no more than three or five days, one *pīṭaka* of silk can produce seven or five strips (*pañca-pāṭa*) for the inner layers.
It consists of three strips of cloth, each one finger-width wide at the outer edge. Along the outer edge there are three rows of stitching. The inner leaves are all sewn together;
this suffices for its function and formal appearance—why rely on anything refined or exquisite? If one wears a *kaṣāya* made of patched rags (*pāṃśukūla*), the intention lies in simplifying affairs:

whether gathering discarded scraps from a heap of refuse or taking what has been cast away in a cemetery, one sews them as soon as they are obtained, using them merely to dispel cold and heat. As for those who say...

The Vinaya states that "bedding" refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*). Upon seeing the prohibition against wild silkworms, some developed a mistaken interpretation, assuming that because the term "prohibited" applied to dharma-robes, they could not be made of silk, and thus diligently sought instead for plain cloth.
Yet they neglected the original text; it turns out these were actually *śayanāsana* (mats/pillows). *Goseya* is the name for silkworms;
when they produce silk, the resulting fabric retains that designation. Since its substance is a precious material, the prohibition against its use was established. As for begging for it oneself...

It is forbidden. To accept what others offer incurs no fault, yet its total use is not permitted; this is a strict regulation for major matters. These various bedding items are not part of the three robes (*tricīvara*). The critique states:

The *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty) says that although Yijing translated the entirety of the Tripiṭaka, he was particularly partial toward revising the Vinaya section.
Thus, while residing in the South Sea, I have sent this text back [to China] specifically to clarify this matter; it is sufficient to show that there are errors and doubts within the *Vinaya-śāstra*.

Now, having carefully examined the various sections of the Vinaya, there are two points of contention: first, refuting [the opponent's view] by means of the meaning according to Yijing; second, refuting it by means of the provisions found in the various Vinayas. Regarding the first point:
in the ninety rules, among the four precepts concerning bedding, the term "sleeping mat" (*mian ru*) is frequently used; it is feared that these are not the three [types of mats].
Regarding robes: as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* within the section on the manufacture of *koseyya* (silk) bedding, it says:
"Koseyya" refers to cotton produced by silkworms; "bedding" refers to a mattress for lying upon. Furthermore, in the newly translated *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, this precept states:
"If a bhikṣu uses new *gośīrṣa* (silk) thread to make bedding and so forth. Additionally, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* regulation states: "If a bhikṣu..."
Regarding the making of new *kauśeya* bedding and so forth, the next three precepts are also called "bedding" (*śayanāsana*).

As for the origin story (*nidāna*) of the precept concerning silk and cotton, the various Vinayas are for the most part identical. Since they all refer to it as "bedding," how could this be a matter of the old translation of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mātṛkā* alone while disregarding the other schools?
Furthermore, there are ten types of clothing materials; as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Clothing consists of ten kinds: woven cloth..."

(Yìjìng [states] that "cut silk" refers to this). There are ten types of garments: cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), *kambala* wool cloth, *kṣauma* linen cloth, *śāṇa* hemp cloth, *śāṭī* cloth, *māñjiṣṭha* cloth, *kāyīra* cloth, *kauśeya* silk cloth, and *cīrṇapaṭṭa* cloth. Among these ten, silk and hemp each account for one;
how could it be that hemp cloth is correct while silk cloth is incorrect? (The former [argument] is refuted). Second, even if [the garment] is torn:

Regarding these three subsequent precepts, one interpretation holds that they pertain to all three robes (*tricīvara*). This is as seen in the *Caturvargika-vinaya* concerning the origin story (*nidāna*) regarding the regulation on bedding made of black sheep’s wool:
"The Licchavis and others frequently practiced sexual misconduct; they would make blankets of pure black sheep’s wool and wear them while walking at night."
He caused people not to see [the transgression]. The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks imitated this by making woolen bedding, whereupon the rule was established [as follows].
Regarding what constitutes no offense, it says: "If one makes a mat, a pillow, a small square sitting-cloth, or a woolen sheet for lying down, there is no offense.
If the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "The Vṛjiputra used black woolen blankets as clothing and bedding; the bhikṣus imitated him. When a householder entered the room..."
He was asked: "What noble person’s belongings are these that the bhikṣus are using? Because of this, he mocked them, saying: "These are the garments of the wealthy elite;
yet the bhikṣus wear robes made of cut patches while seeking the path to non-action (asaṃskṛta), and now they act like this. It was on account of this that the Buddha established the rule.

Regarding what constitutes a transgression, it is the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Sifen lü*), even concerning items such as bedding mats. This is within the section on bedding and seating for the fourth and sixth years, after the Buddha had already established the regulations.

There was a sick bhikṣu suffering from thirst who wished to travel among the people. He had a piece of discarded bedding (pāṃsukūla-śayanāsana), but because it was heavy, he could not carry it with him.

He informed the Buddha, who further established a rule: "If one has not yet completed six years [of using an old robe] and does not discard it, yet makes a new one, this is prohibited except by formal authorization through a *saṃgha-karman*.

This is corroborated by the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which records that [the rule] originated from imitating someone walking at night while wearing a black woolen blanket. Furthermore, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*...

Regarding the regulation on clothing: one must not violate the middle [rule]. Furthermore, he ordered the making of a bedding mat (*śayanāsana*). If it was originally a bedding mat, why would it be permitted again?
Moreover, because when traveling among humans one cannot carry heavy items, he had them exchange their heavy ones for new, light ones to carry, using the three robes themselves as bedding.
This is found in the *Vinaya-kośa* (律抄), and there is indeed reason for this; this is a case of leniency. As for those who say it violates [the rules], I shall now examine this in detail.
Regarding bedding and requisites: even if these are the three robes (*tricīvara*), they are specifically the felt (*kambala*) three robes. Therefore, one must not mix them with silk-cotton (*tūla*).

Among materials such as wool (*vāla*) or cotton cloth (*kārpāsa*), if they have been processed [into felt], it is permissible to cut them and mix them with clay to plaster walls; this does not constitute an offense.

If they are the formal felt three robes, they should be made using three parts black and two parts white, with four parts coarse hair. This robe is permitted to be kept for six years; thus it is known.
In this context, it is permitted only to make robes from felt; making them from mixed silk-cotton is not permitted.

Furthermore, there is no separate textual regulation stating that one may not use pure cotton or silk to make the three robes (*tricīvara*). This is because, among the ten types of robes, the first is a silk robe.

Moreover, regarding the subsequent instruction to dye [robes] into three kinds of discolored hues (*kāṣāya*), it states that one "should dye hemp robes, silk robes, and so forth. Based on these two points—one affirming and one negating—it follows that silk is indeed [permitted].

This is a practice established by the Buddha for general use; the Vinaya contains no textual prohibition against it. However, since ancient times, it has not been universally practiced, and for a period, practitioners have mutually refused to permit it.
I hope that those of broad learning will examine this more closely. Provided it does not contravene the Vinaya, there is no need for rigid enforcement.

The *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) states: "One must not wear silk or brocade from the East. This shares the same intent as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* passage cited in the aforementioned Vinaya commentary (*lǜchāo*).
This is a Mahāyāna universal prohibition concerning both internal and external garments; it applies to all practitioners and does not permit their use.

It is not like the Vinaya regulations, which pertain specifically to the three robes (*tricīvara*). One must not use a general rule to justify a restricted one, especially given that there are [current instances of such use].
To wear silk and damask on the inside while wearing coarse cloth on the outside not only shows a lack of familiarity with the Vinaya texts, but also a failure to understand the scriptural teachings.
Regarding the four types [of robes], "for one's own personal use" refers to keeping a single bowl for one’s own use. As for the phrase "always carrying it oneself," the *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"Each person makes their own bowl-sack, places the bowl inside, and carries it themselves. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* says: "To protect..."
The alms bowl is like the pupil of the eye; it should be placed and kept in a proper location. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"If it is difficult to hold while grasped by hand, one should make a bag to contain it, tie its opening, and carry it slung over the shoulder, tucking the bowl under the arm with its opening facing outward. The *Sudarsana-vibhasa* states: "The earthenware bowl-bag is strung over the left shoulder;
however, when begging for food, it should be held in the palms of the hands. The reason for carrying it oneself is because of [the need to provide] the bowl to the *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person)."
While he was begging for alms, a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) threw medicine into his bowl; because the bhikṣu died as a result, [the Buddha] established the rule that one must hold [the bowl] oneself.

Regarding the term "proper vessel" (saṃbhoga-pātra): the Madhyama Āgama states that "bowl" (pātra) is also called a "proper vessel," so named because it accords with the substance, color, and measure [of a monk].

As for "substance," the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says there are essentially two types: earthenware bowls and iron bowls. (According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are six types of bowls, namely: iron bowls, *sumana* [bowls],...)

The *guo-ba* (country bowl), the *wugala-guo-ba*, the *youjiyu-guo-ba*, the black bowl, and the red bowl—these names merely indicate the countries from which they originate; in essence, they do not deviate from being made of clay or iron. Wooden bowls belong to non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*), stone bowls belong only to the Buddha, and vessels made of various jewels belong to householders.
Monks differ from these; they possess only bowls of earthenware or iron. Regarding the two colors, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that they should be fired to produce black or red.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a bowl fired to the color of a peacock’s throat or the color of a pigeon is in accordance with the Dharma (an iron bowl may be fired five times for use, while an earthenware bowl requires only two firings).

Regarding the three measures (*trīṇi mātrāṇi*): the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that the large bowl holds three and a half *dōng* (斗), the small bowl holds one and a half *dōng*, and the medium bowl may be inferred accordingly.
As for this *dōng*, its capacity is not fixed; this Vinaya was translated during the Yao Qin period, and the *dōng* of that country’s Jizhou (姬周) standard corresponds to the Tang *dōng*.
The superior bowl has a capacity of one *dou*; the inferior has five *shuan*. The measurements in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* are the same as those in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

[The above are excerpts from the Vinaya. Nanshan (Daoxuan) refutes this, stating: "Although the fixed measurements of the various schools are not uniform, they mostly take three *dou* or one and a half *dou* as the limit.
However, the name of this vessel should be 'proper vessel' (*yìngqí*), which must be established according to the teachings. The Vinaya says: 'Measure the belly.'"

One eats according to one's capacity and wears clothing according to one's body, seeking only to satisfy one's needs. While these matters may vary according to circumstances, they must necessarily conform to the authentic teachings. However, let us now examine this in detail.
The reason the capacity of the alms bowl is of such a size is established based on the physical proportions of the Buddha and the people of his time.

If we consider the people of the present day, whose stature is somewhat shorter and smaller, it would indeed be appropriate to measure the bowl according to their own stomachs. As stated in the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (Buddhacarita-sūtra), the Buddha...
The Buddha was one zhang and six chi tall. Devadatta was one zhang, five chi, and four cun tall. Nanda was one zhang, five chi, and four cun tall.
Ānanda was one zhang, five chi, and two cun tall. The physical stature of the other disciples can likewise be known.

Only Śāriputra was called the "diminutive bhikṣu," whereas those with other names were called "magnificent" because their physical stature was large and tall; thus, the size of their almsbowls was also large, a tradition that has continued down to the present day.
One should fashion [one's robes] according to the measure of one’s own belly; how could it possibly be based on the standards of the Buddha’s lifetime?

Previously, people merely doubted the dimensions [of the robes] without considering how they should be adapted to the person. Thus, this is explained for the sake of thorough understanding (although Nanshan follows the scriptural measurements, even he has not yet reached such merit).

Among the five [types of requisites], the internal refers to food and drink, while the external refers to clothing and various other necessities. Since one sustains oneself through alms, one does not engage in worldly management or hoarding.

One does not employ expedients that lead to faults in other lives. Furthermore, since one has already sought out food and clothing for oneself and managed them, one thereby subdues and treats with contempt the body and mind (the *Zhufa* [Treatise on Abiding in the Dharma] mentions only "begging for food," which may not reflect the intent of this treatise). Among the six [practices], one generally employs wisdom to contemplate the five preceding matters.

Among the seven [stages], the former involves a general contemplation of the external and a general treatment of the internal; thus, by contemplating the external and treating the internal, they are swiftly extinguished. This is the inquiry into their arising.

Regarding the subtle affliction of pride (*māna*), the subtle is used as an illustration for the coarse, as has already been explained previously. However, the preceding sections of the sūtra text each become progressively more excellent.
Herein, the treatment of pride—which directly obstructs the Path to Enlightenment—is intended to cause it to be swiftly extinguished.

In terms of abandoning the afflictions, once the defilements are severed and one enters the Path, one attains liberation; therefore, the text next states: "The person who has entered the Path, for the sake of liberation..."

Practicing alms-gathering is not merely to prevent the initial resolve from arising even momentarily; rather, while the initial resolve subdues gross afflictions, this practice causes the subtle ones to be extinguished.

Furthermore, since all three stages of treating the afflictions demonstrate the Noble Path—and entering the Path constitutes the supramundane—the subsequent section clarifies the supramundane merits [of this practice].
(This critique of the method of abiding refers to the practitioner at the stage of the initial resolve.)
Second, "the rest" refers to the comparison and exhortation to abandon [pride]. This means that even a layperson (*avadātavasana*) should not be arrogant. Thus, the *Yi* (Book of Changes) says:

"The way of humanity detests fullness and loves humility. The *Li* (Book of Rites) says: "Arrogance must not be allowed to grow; desire must not be indulged. This is precisely what constitutes such a comparison.
Therefore, in making this comparison, one should not give rise to arrogance. Regarding the phrase "merit of the prior limit," it refers to the sutra...
This refers to "leaving home" (renunciation). If one gives rise to arrogance, one does not even equal the dharma of a layperson; how then could one accomplish the merit of leaving home?
Merit regarding the future limit refers precisely to entering the Path. It does not mean that merely leaving home is called entering the Path.
This is called "one who enters the Way," because they enter the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). The preceding section states that this is the intrinsic nature of wisdom;
the subsequent section states that during the stage of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), all [terms] refer to the Noble Path being entered.

It is precisely because of this path entered at the later limit (*paścimakoṭi*) that it is not the former limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). (The *Zhufa yaoji* says: "The merit of the former limit refers to leaving home and entering the Way. This not only shows a lack of understanding of this meaning, but is also confused regarding both the preceding and following contexts. Thus it is established.
If one rises [from this state], it cannot be called entering the Way. This means that while one has left home in the past (the anterior limit), one enters the Way only later (the posterior limit);
all such merits are obstructed by arrogance. Furthermore, leaving home and entering the Way are fundamentally for the sake of liberation; thus, liberation is the primary objective.
The character "jì" (際) is pronounced with the second tone, following the rhyme of "hú" and "jiāng."

The third is the obstacle of flattery and crookedness. Next, the lower [obstacles] are explained. First, the chapter is introduced. The previous two obstacles both concern using external things to treat internal afflictions;

they involve treating internal delusions by means of external matters. Here, however, it does not refer to anything else, but directly cites the contrariety of one's own mind to the path that is entered.
Because flattery and crookedness are contrary to the straight path, they follow next.

Second, the citation of the sutra; third, the commentary and its explanation—these three. Regarding the section beginning with "The treatise says": first, there is a general indication of the antidote and that which is to be remedied.

As for the phrase "the fundamental straightforward mind," it is stated below that "the straightforward mind is the root of the bodhicitta. This refers to its being the foundation for entering the Path.

This serves as the antidote, while flattery and crookedness are that which is to be remedied. That is to say, to deceive others through pretense and to feign artificial deportment out of sycophancy and crookedness.
Nature. Flattery (*śāṭhya*) is precisely crookedness; therefore, it is called "flattery-crookedness. Second, the specific demonstration of the two:
the object of treatment (*vipakṣa*) and the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*). Regarding the body, first is the object of treatment. As stated in the *Dharmameghā-sūtra*:

"Ordinary fools are themselves ignorant of the movements and functions of their three karmas, yet they still deceive their own minds. Excessive courtesy and a supple countenance constitute flattery of the body. Clever speech and artful words constitute [flattery of speech]."

Flattery of speech is flattery of the mind through the employment of expedient stratagems; these three are all crooked and deviant, yet they originate in the mind, and for this reason it is simply called "mind" (*citta*).

To say that one "contradicts them" means that the Way (*mārga*) is precisely what they are not; since the Way is not crooked or deviant, one stands in opposition to them. Furthermore, the following two [qualities] serve as their remedies.
The Sūtra states "uprightness," which directly remedies flattery and crookedness; therefore, it is called the "remedy for the obstacle of contradicting the Way."

Third, showing that one must instead offer admonitions and exhortations. Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "Again, moreover": first, it shows that one should not act contrary [to the path].

The repeated mention above of "factors of the path" (*mārga-aṅga*) refers to the time of entering the factors of the path; therefore, at the time of entering the factors of the path, one should not be sycophantic or crooked. Regarding the passage beginning with "In this regard": [it follows that...]
A separate explanation of *śāṭhya* (deceit). "Deceit" (*śāṭha*) means taking the false for the true; as Mencius said: "A gentleman may be deceived by [an opponent] using their own methods.
"Deception" (*māyā*) means taking the empty for the real; as Vasubandhu said: "For the sake of profit and reputation, one feigns the possession of virtue;
its nature is that of guile and fraud. These all involve a lack of sincerity between mind and speech. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Because the mind and words are straightforward, it is thus."

From beginning to end, its status remains constant; in the interim, there is no element of deviousness. As for the others, they are inferior. Second, this accords with the admonition to be straightforward and upright.
Since straightforwardness and uprightness constitute the very foundation of the Way, one ought to rectify the mind.
III. The Section on Cultivating the Supramundane Qualities of Great Beings is divided into two parts. "Having already explained [the preceding]" and so forth:

first, the conclusion of the previous section and the introduction of the subsequent one are presented as a general indication. The former was described in terms of the karma and suffering to be remedied, and thus was called "mundane"; this [section], however, is described in terms of the qualities to be cultivated.

Therefore, it is called "transcending the world. Although these meanings mutually interpenetrate, they are categorized according to their predominant characteristics; hence, this section follows next. Regarding the eight merits, the following provides a general indication. The *Yanyi* states:
"The Eight Arousals of the Great Men are fully elucidated in the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Upadeśa*). First, few desires; second, contentment."
Third, tranquility; fourth, diligence; fifth, right mindfulness; sixth, right concentration; seventh, right wisdom; eighth, non-proliferation; ninth, nirvāṇa;
and tenth, adding the two [preceding] to make ten. "Good son, if a bodhisattva accomplishes these ten dharmas, although they see the Buddha-nature, they do not perceive it clearly.
The first seven are as above. The eighth is liberation. The ninth is praising liberation. The tenth..."

They teach and transform sentient beings by means of *nirvāṇa*. However, according to the present treatise, since the first seven [stages] constitute the skillful means of nurturing and the eighth constitutes the ultimate accomplishment, the first seven are the cause and the eighth is the fruit.

This is because the Sūtra, in terms of the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the attainment of the bliss of tranquility, refers to the very meaning of liberation; thus, they differ only in terminology. Furthermore, although two [stages] have been added, the ninth is...

This praises the eighth merit. Since the tenth involves transformation through birth by means of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), the preceding eight constitute the correct practice as one's own cause and fruit;

the latter two praise transformation that does not abide in one's own fruit but transforms others. This is the distinction between compassion and wisdom (as stated in the *Sūtra on the Eight Great Persons' Awakenings*, which concludes:

"Mounting the ship of the Dharma-body, one reaches the shore of Nirvāṇa, then returns to saṃsāra to deliver sentient beings"—this is identical in intent to the latter two [merits] regarding Nirvāṇa). If one were to explain the preceding eight:
The aspects of practice are largely identical to those in the present sutra. However, if one refers to the *Sutra on the Eight Great Persons' Awakening* (one fascicle, two folios;

translated by An Shigao), there are slight differences in terminology and meaning. Regarding the eight points in that sutra: first, awakening to impermanence (its meaning is the same as the sixth, "Right Concentration," for the sutra states: "Because one knows the characteristics of arising and ceasing"; the treatise states:

"Because one contemplates the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death"—this is the characteristic of worldly impermanence). Second, awakening to the suffering of excessive desire (identical to the first in the present text). Third, awakening to the knowledge of contentment (identical to the second in the present text).
4. Awakening to and cognizing laziness (the same as the fourth in the present system). 5. Awakening to and cognizing ignorance (the same as the seventh in the present system). 6.

Awakening to and cognizing the suffering of craving (this refers to mindfulness of giving and the equality of enemies and kin; it is the same as the fifth in the present system, as it involves not forgetting various merits and practicing the fearlessness-giving). 7. Awakening to and cognizing the faults of the five desires (this refers to renunciation, the holy life, and so forth).

This corresponds to the third [stage], Quiescence (*śānti*). The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Quiescence has two aspects: first, the joy of renunciation; second, the joy of quiescence. This joy of quiescence is precisely the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The eighth [stage], the Extinction of Discursive Proliferation (*aprapañca*), corresponds to the meaning of the eightfold awakening from the burning intensity of birth and death.

This means that because one resolves to take upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings, one attains the joy of extinction while not abiding in extinction. One enters into birth and death to undergo suffering, for one knows that the root of suffering is originally quiescent and that sentient beings are primordially abiding in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "The self-nature is far removed. The *Sūtra* says: "These eight matters are that which all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and great beings have awakened to;
they practice them with vigor," and so forth. Although the assigned meanings are the same, the terminology differs slightly and the sequence is also distinct;

however, generally speaking, these eight awakenings are identical in this regard. Since their names, meanings, and sequence coincide with those of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this section of the present *sūtra*...
The concluding titles at the end of each section constitute the formal title and meaning of this scripture; fundamentally, it is identical to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

However, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa has now prefixed this general title to the beginning of these eight sections so that the distinct meanings may find their point of reference, thereby making known that [the author] is one of the eight great enlightened persons.
Regarding the abiding of the Dharma, it is also said here: although the teaching belongs to the Hīnayāna, the treatise judges it as a Mahāyāna practice. If this is so, then regarding the *Nirvāṇa*...

What has been stated should also be considered minor. However, when observing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Eight Great Aspirations of a Mahāsattva*, although these concern the practice of Bodhisattvas, they also universally apply to the Two Vehicles as they advance toward the Great Way. (The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Having attained the four fruits, one does not cease in the mind from seeking Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;

this is called diligence," and so forth. The *Sūtra on the Eight Aspirations* says: "If a disciple of the Buddha recites these eight matters, in every thought-moment they shall extinguish immeasurable sins and advance toward Bodhi, swiftly ascending to Perfect Enlightenment. This is also consistent with the intent of the present treatise.

Nevertheless, although this is primarily intended for Bodhisattvas, it also extends to include those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). This is the same meaning as the previous explanation regarding the bhikṣu.

Moreover, since the present treatise states that "great beings always employ [this]," it indicates that this applies exclusively to Bodhisattvas; conversely, it shows that those who do not always employ it—namely, those who have attained only a partial realization—inclusive of the two vehicles.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of four permutations concerning contentment and fewness of desires, stating: "There are those who have few desires but are not called 'content'."
There are those who possess contentment but are not called "few in desire," namely the *pratyekabuddhas*. There are those who possess both fewness of desire and contentment, namely the *arhats*.

There are those who possess fewness of desire but lack contentment, namely the *bodhisattvas*. (The first two phrases refer to the Small Vehicle; they are distinct and do not overlap, representing partial attainment.

The third phrase refers to the *arhat*, who possesses both [qualities], thus citing their skillful means. The fourth phrase refers to the *bodhisattva*, who extensively cultivates all practices and is thus neither "insufficient" nor "few in desire"). The above...

Regarding the meaning: thus we know that Guishan’s claim that all three vehicles are called "great persons" (mahāpuruṣa) is an overly broad statement and does not reflect the intent of the sūtras or śāstras.

Zhuzhao’s claim that the term "great" distinguishes the [bodhisattva] from the small [vehicle], and thus does not apply to the two vehicles, is an overly narrow statement and likewise does not reflect the intent of the śāstra.

Xuanye’s claim that it refers to those in the two vehicles as well as the Buddha-stage—wherein it is said that after a śrāvaka has attained a small fruit, they proceed toward great bodhi—is [correct].
Because it is "great. To realize this, the term "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa) generally refers to those of the three vehicles; yet this is not the intended meaning of the sūtras and śāstras.

In the sūtras and śāstras, the name "Great Person" is applied specifically to Bodhisattvas. This does not preclude the inclusion of those who advance from the Lesser Vehicle, nor does it mean that the Lesser Vehicle itself is called "Great.

Furthermore, it does not mean that the three vehicles within the Mahāyāna are collectively termed "Mahāyāna" (for although there are three vehicles within the Mahāyāna, they are internally distinguished as Great and Small). As for that Buddha...
The *Dilun* [treatise] states that those of small fruition advance toward the Great [Vehicle]. This is as cited above from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Entering the Great from the Small.

By citing those skillful means, once one has entered the Great, they are no longer called followers of the Small Vehicle; this further clarifies that "Great Persons" refers exclusively to Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, when the treatise says, "constantly self-awakening and examining," it means constantly using this for self-reflection; it is not spoken in reference to self-benefit alone. Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, as in the ninety... [etc.]
"Commending transformation" clarifies the benefit of others. If this is so, are these eight [perfections] not practices for one's own benefit? The answer is:
it is not that they lack the benefit of others; however, with respect to these eight, they are specifically designated as the awakening to oneself alone.
The terms "nurturing" (*poṣaṇa*) and so forth are sequential phrases, as will be understood later in the seventh section.

Second, based on the cited sūtra, there is a detailed explanation of the eight [faults]. First, regarding "the fault of having many desires," there are two parts: first, the citation of the sūtra; second, the commentary’s explanation.

Regarding the commentary, starting from "The treatise says" below, there is first a general indication. As for the phrase "the fault of having many desires," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "There are three kinds of desire."
First, evil desire; second, great desire; third, the desire for desire. Regarding evil desire:

if a bhikṣu gives rise to covetous thoughts, desiring that all sentient beings—those of the highest rank—should have the entire Saṃgha follow behind him, that the fourfold assembly should all provide him with offerings and respect, and that kings, ministers, and others should likewise honor him, so that he may obtain the most excellent and sublime [attainments].
Clothing, food, drink, and the like, which serve as the desires of birth and death, are called "evil desires.

If a bhikṣu wishes for the fourfold assembly to know that he has attained the stages (*bhūmi*), attained *bodhi*, or attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], for the sake of gain and offerings, this is called "great desire.

If a bhikṣu wishes to be born in the Brahma heavens, or even to become a Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) or one of the Kṣatriya clans, and to attain sovereignty over all such things, [this is also great desire].
Because of gain and honor, it is called the "desire for desire. If one is not harmed by these three kinds of evil desires, this is called having few desires.
"Desire" refers to the twenty-five types of craving; to be without these twenty-five cravings is called having few desires.
This also includes the faults of excessive desire within this context. Because one does not now seek the three superior types of desire, it is called the "merit of non-seeking.
Second, there are two distinct explanations. Within these, the first is a general explanation; the second, beginning with "First," is a specific explanation. Regarding the person of excessive desire:
This phrase refers to the person by way of their desires; it has not yet been correlated with the three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). The same applies to those of few desires mentioned below.

"Seeking much" is karma; the character "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is the fruit; and the character "affliction" (*upāyāsa*) is the afflictive delusion (*kleśa*). Therefore, the subsequent commentary explains suffering and affliction as follows:

Regarding "affliction" (*daurmanasya*) herein: it refers to the fault of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because it arises from suffering. Since affliction arises subsequent to suffering, it demonstrates that affliction further gives rise to karma, and karma in turn induces suffering;
thus, it is said to "revolve without ceasing. Now, as for why the treatise does not explain the two characters "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and "affliction" (*daurmanasya*) at this point:
the intention is to provide a mutual abbreviation with the subsequent section of the treatise. Since the latter part states, "arising from suffering," [the former is understood].
"Affliction (*daurmanasya*). This implies that this revolving does not cease; herein, the revolving does not cease because affliction arises from suffering below.

(To pair "abiding in dharmas" with the fruit of suffering and "having much desire" with the afflictions is a grave error. Among these two, being without seeking and without desire is precisely the departure from karma, as cited above.
The three kinds of desire are all false karma; since one now departs from these, the sutra states there is no such affliction, and one is free from suffering and affliction.

The second is delusion (*moha*). Since those with many desires seek much, their suffering and affliction (*duḥkha* and *upāyāsa*) are many; whereas now, those with few desires have no seeking or desire, and thus lack this ailment.

Therefore, we know that this "ailment" specifically refers to suffering and affliction (since both *duḥkha* and *upāyāsa* are termed "ailments," the interpretation applied here to the *Dharmasthiti-sūtra* is also erroneous).

Among the three [types of persons], the Sūtra says: "One should cultivate fewness of desires. This refers to one's own cause. How much more so for one who has already attained fewness of desires? This follows upon that.

Moreover, it is because this manifests the ability to give rise to the fruits of the merits of the myriad practices. This constitutes the characteristic of the causal and resultant arising through habituation.

Since the cause of having few desires is that which gives rise [to results], then immeasurable merit is that which is produced. In terms of the meaning of what is produced, it is called a "result. Therefore, it is said:

"Because one accomplishes immeasurable practices" (abiding in the Dharma by taking immeasurable practices and merits as cause and result; nor is it otherwise). Among the four [categories], this is awakening.

Because the first three obstacles are ultimately non-existent, "few desires" characterizes the person. Being without guile means there are no afflictions (*kleśa*). Not seeking the favor of others means there is no karma (*karman*).
Not being dragged by the sense faculties (*indriya*) means there is no suffering (*duḥkha*). When the faculties encounter their objects, they are dragged along to produce consciousness;
therefore, much desire leads to suffering. Now, since one is not dragged, the fruit of suffering does not exist. Among these five, there is ultimate accomplishment. That is to say:

Because the Sūtra contains [the teaching of] *nirvāṇa*. However, this is the inverse of the preceding section. By being free from the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), these three virtues (*guṇa*) are established.

That is to say, by being free from the crookedness mentioned previously, the mind is utterly tranquil; in meaning, this corresponds to the inversion of afflictions (*kleśa*), which is the virtue of *prajñā* (i.e., non-conceptual wisdom).

Therefore, one is suddenly startled. This reverses the previous state of seeking favor through crooked means; thus, there is no sorrow or fear (whereas previously it was said that seeking favor through crookedness is merely for the sake of deception, and thus entails sorrow and fear; now this is the opposite).
In meaning, this corresponds to the reversal of the karma of bondage; it is the dharma of liberation.

Because one is no longer dragged by the sense faculties as before, there is "constant sufficiency with remainder" (whereas being dragged by the faculties leads to the suffering of desire—namely, the burning and constant suffering of lack). In meaning, this corresponds to the reversal of the dharma of the fruit of suffering to become the virtue of the body.
Since one practices few desires, the three types of defilement are reversed to form these three virtues. Therefore, one who possesses few desires is fully endowed [with them].

Regarding these three virtues (*guṇa*), there is *nirvāṇa*. To maintain that *nirvāṇa* corresponds to the virtue of the *dharmakāya*, and that "serene fearlessness" (*tathatā-vaiśāradya*) corresponds to both [the virtues of] *prajñā*, is entirely contrary to the intent of the treatise. Since *nirvāṇa* possesses all three virtues, how could it be separately assigned to the *dharmakāya* alone?
As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If the three dots were separate, they would not form the letter 'I' (*ī*). I am also like this. Thus it is understood.
The dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa; the body of the Tathāgata is also not nirvāṇa; mahāprajñā is also not nirvāṇa.

If these three dharmas were distinct from one another, they would likewise not be nirvāṇa. Now, if nirvāṇa is uniquely equated with the Dharmakāya, how could it be established as nirvāṇa if the three dharmas are distinct?
If it is argued that because nirvāṇa is the ultimate teaching, it must possess the three virtues (triguṇa) to be so named...

Regarding *nirvāṇa*: the present sutra is not like that. As for the point that it does not preclude a separate correlation, this sutra simply refers to *nirvāṇa* by way of possessing the three virtues;
it does not do so by taking one [virtue] as being immediately the three. This clarifies that they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct, and so forth.

The sutra states, "This is called having few desires," which concludes the naming. All subsequent instances follow this pattern. Nevertheless, although this chapter is the most prominent in both sutras and śāstras, the application of these dharmas has been lost.

What is the essential meaning? [It concerns] the three merits of awareness (*jñāna*). First is the heading of the section. The preceding [section] concerned distancing oneself from the affairs of others; this [section] concerns distancing oneself from one's own [affairs].

Therefore, it follows next. Second is the citation of the sūtra. Third is the commentary’s explanation, which has two parts. Regarding the passage beginning with "The treatise says," the first part provides a general indication: all eight are termed "awareness" (*bodhi*). Alone...
This is called "the one who possesses awareness. For a sutra states, "One should contemplate contentment. Contemplation is that which can awaken, while contentment is that which is awakened to.
Because both the subject and object are present, it is called "accomplishing the practice of contentment."
Second, the detailed explanation of the two [aspects]. First, showing that the antidote and the object to be remedied are distinct. First, the actual explanation.

Regarding the section "The Treatise on Antidotes" (*Upāya-kauśalya-śāstra*), first is the remedy for the causes and effects of suffering. Within this, the phrase "the faults of afflictions" (*kleśa-doṣa*) uses the character *nǎo* (惱) from the Sūtra;
