this refers to the faults and calamities of the afflictions (*kleśa*), and does not mean that the character *guò* (過) refers to karma. The correct meaning has been explained above. (Regarding the *Zhùfǎ*, the interpretation that assigns the character *guò* to karma significantly misses the intent of the Treatise. Furthermore, this Sūtra says: "All...")

[The opponent says: "It is suffering and affliction (*duḥkha*). Since he has already been designated as one of the Three Lords of the Śākyas (*tridaśa-śākyādhipati*), and it was previously stated that there is much suffering and affliction, why is [suffering] alone assigned here? Therefore, both instances are erroneous; this clearly shows that [the opponent] does not understand the purport of the treatise."
Furthermore, it is said below that these two constitute the cause and fruit of purity. Contentment is the cause of purity; wealth, happiness, and security are the fruits of purity.

As for what is called the "dharma of cultivation," this refers precisely to the dharma of contentment. The Sūtra states that this [contentment] is both the cause of purity and, moreover, the fruit of purity.
Why is this? One who is content, though possessing great wealth, remains happy even while sleeping on the ground; they do not [suffer].

Because one desires to attain security, contentment is itself the state of wealth and happiness, and the state of security; thus it is said, "it is precisely this. The subsequent sutra also addresses these three meanings.

To abide in the Dharma means that, because there is no greed or affliction, wealth and happiness serve as the cause, while liberation from the three miserable realms and transcendence of the two deaths constitute the fruit of security.

To lose [this understanding] would be far removed from the truth. If one were to distinguish and eliminate confusion as follows: [The text continues with the specific distinctions regarding the causes and fruits.]

Regarding the distinction: because that which is to be remedied is the same (that which is to be remedied is suffering and affliction; it is not different in meaning from "various sufferings and afflictions"). Here, the distinction is made solely by way of abandoning [the desire for] both self and others.
If one asks, within *nirvāṇa*, what is the difference between "having few desires" (*alpeccha*) and "being content" (*saṃtuṣṭa*), the Buddha said:
"Having few desires" means not seeking and not taking; "being content" means that when one has obtained even a little, the mind feels no regret. Having few desires...

Regarding "few desires": to have few things desired. Regarding "contentment": to act solely for the sake of the Dharma, with a mind free from anxiety and affliction, and not seeking future objects of desire;
this is called having few desires. To obtain things without attachment is called contentment. Not seeking honor and respect is called having few desires.
To obtain things without accumulating them is called contentment (there are four further phrases as cited above). Now, regarding *nirvāṇa*...

Although "pāna" has many meanings, they do not go beyond the distinction between self and other within this context. Their correspondence can be understood through reflection. Second, showing the distinctions of contentment (saṃtuṣṭi).
[The text states: "Furthermore," which first indicates the heading; "First," which introduces the second part of the explanation.

In both instances where it asks "What kind?"—as in the case of "abiding in the middle"—it should be stated: "In what respect is there contentment in enjoyment? In what respect is there no contentment?"

This refers to the experience of sufficiency. Because the two states of being content and being discontented are different, they are called "distinctions. The following two cases should be understood by analogy.
However, these are all phrases used to introduce the questions, which are then answered by means of the Sūtra. As in the answer to the first:

although one who is content finds joy even when sleeping on the ground, one who is discontented does not find satisfaction even in heaven. The following two cases are likewise so. These are the three distinctions.

[This] explains and establishes the preceding purity of cause and effect. As for [the text] stating "each pair" (*ekaika-dvandva*) regarding the abiding dharmas, it is because it demonstrates the meaning of differentiation; thus, [your objection] appears not to have understood the intent of the treatise.

This chapter is particularly mistaken in its intent; it even goes so far as to reproach those of the past for destroying the Dharma and deceiving people, failing to realize that such faults return to oneself. Within this [teaching], there is no lack of self-benefit, for one desires to lead others and thus possesses self-benefit.
Because one is moved by compassion for others through the practice of contentment, there is benefit for both self and others.
Since one has already known oneself and pities others, both forms of benefit are present.
Record of the Commentary on the *Śāsanāntara-sūtra*, Scroll II.
Written with utmost care by Jingque on the second day before the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the second year of the Renchen cycle of the Zhengde era.
Record of the Commentary on the *Śāsanāntara-sūtra*, Scroll III.
Composed by Xia'an Guanfu. Part Three:
The Merit of Renunciation. First, the heading. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the sequence as follows:

"To distance oneself from all worldly affairs is called 'having few desires' (*alpeccha*). Once one has gone forth [into homelessness], not giving rise to regret is called 'contentment' (*saṃtuṣṭi*)."
Having attained contentment, one dwells near secluded places and stays far removed from clamor; this is called tranquility.
Those who lack contentment do not delight in seclusion, whereas those who possess contentment always rejoice in emptiness and stillness; therefore, it follows next.

Second, the citation of the sutra; third, the commentary explaining the two [points]. Regarding the section beginning with "The treatise says," first, the categories are established and the underlying intent is revealed.

*Nirvāṇa* is termed "quiescence" (*śānti*) in reference to that which is capable of distancing itself from defilement. Since clamor and bustle are what are to be distanced, the term "distancing" (*dūrī-bhāva*) here encompasses both the agent and the object, and thus it is called "distancing."
Regarding the phrase "the self-nature is far removed," etc.: persons and phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; their nature is eternally free from clamor, hence it is called "emergence by essence.

When one abandons manifold thoughts and they cease, body and mind are finally at peace; this is called "emergence through skillful means. Because one delights in the crowds and undergoes affliction, being entangled by the view of self, it is called "constant bondage."

The second part, the explanation according to the gates, has three sections. First, the gate of the natural absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vigama-mukha*). Under the heading "The intrinsic nature of the treatise," the first section provides a general indication:
because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally empty, one employs this emptiness of intrinsic nature to remedy the four obstacles.

The second part, the detailed explanation, has four sections. First is the "lower" section. Regarding the first, the obstacle of attachment to the mark of a self (*ātman*): this obstacle generally comprises two types of self.

The first refers to the conception of a governing master within the aggregates (*skandha*), which is called the "mark of the personal self" (*pudgala-ātman*). The second refers to the conception that the substance of the aggregates possesses a real intrinsic nature, which is the "mark of the phenomenal self" (*dharma-ātman*).
Now, according to the Mahāyāna, the teaching of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is presented as the antidote. Its emptiness, signlessness, and...

The vows are called the three gates of emptiness (also known as the three gates of samādhi). The *Kongmu* states: "When based on the object, they are called 'gates'; when based on the observing wisdom, they are called 'samādhis. They are also called the three liberations (*vimokṣa*).

Cultivating them initially constitutes samādhi; completing them finally constitutes liberation. Here, we are specifically referring to the three gates of emptiness; thus, it says: the emptiness of dharma-non-self, the emptiness of signlessness, and the emptiness of wishlessness.

The *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*, in its section on the inclusion of the sixteen aspects of the four truths within the three liberations, states: "Within the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), there are the sixteen aspects and the three [liberations]."

The gates of liberation mutually encompass one another. Question: How many modes of practice (*ākāra*) are subsumed under emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? Answer: Two; namely, the mode of emptiness and the mode of non-self (*anātman*). Question:

How many modes of practice are subsumed under wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)? Answer: Six; namely, the mode of impermanence (*anitya*), the mode of suffering (*duḥkha*)—which includes the aforementioned two [modes of emptiness and non-self, making these four modes within the Truth of Suffering]—the mode of cause (*hetu*), the mode of origination (*samudaya*), the mode of production (*jāti*), and the mode of condition (*pratyaya*)—these four being the four modes within the Truth of Origination. This is because, by means of them, there is nothing sought within the three realms. Question:
How many aspects (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the signless (*animitta*)? Answer: Eight. That is, the eight aspects of cessation and the path.

This is because they cannot produce any signs. (Regarding the four aspects of cessation: first, the aspect of cessation, meaning it is free from the fetters of afflictions; second, the aspect of tranquility, meaning it is free from the fetters of the characteristics of suffering; third, the aspect of excellence, meaning it is free from the fetters of the two higher realms;

fourth, the aspect of departure, meaning it never regresses and is supremely secure. Regarding the four aspects of the path: first, the aspect of the path, meaning it is the route by which noble ones realize suchness; second, the aspect of accordance, meaning it purifies the afflictions; third, the aspect of practice, meaning it awakens to the true meaning; fourth, the aspect of transcendence, meaning it proceeds toward the path of true permanence.)

The present treatise states: "That which is 'quiescent' (śānta) is because of the emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Here, emptiness is itself quiescence; this precisely corresponds to the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatācaryā*) in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Its demonstration of the selflessness of phenomena is precisely that practice of the selflessness of phenomena. Regarding its explanation of emptiness, it says: "There are three kinds of emptiness:

namely, the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)—this is observed with respect to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is definitively non-existent; [second,] the emptiness of suchness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*)—this is observed with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);..."

The contemplation of nature (*prakṛti-vipaśyanā*): because all that is thus conceptualized is non-existent. The true nature (*tattva*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*): this refers to the contemplation of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), for it is the very emptiness of true reality. Regarding his explanation of "selflessness" (*anātman*):

it is called the characteristic of selflessness because the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*) are absent. Therefore, the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) that "all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self.

[Critical Evaluation: Both of the above refer to the emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-śūnyatā*). As for "the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), it is characterized by the absence of marks (*animitta*).
Regarding "because it is empty": this is because it is subsumed under the eight aspects of the cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-aṣṭāṅga*) within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

That text states: "Because it cannot produce any characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)," which refers to the present unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the statement "peaceful and blissful" and "because it is empty of grasping, abandoning, and aspiration":

this is also consistent with its subsumption under the six aspects (*ṣaḍākāra*) in that same text. That text states: "Because it has nothing to seek within the three realms," which corresponds to the present meaning of being without grasping or abandoning. By means of these three...

The realms are without stability; one does not seek or desire the three realms. The three higher emptinesses are all contemplations of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which remedy the two types of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).
Regarding the second pair, below, there is the obstacle of "mine" (*mama-kāra*). This "mine" has two aspects: internal and external.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that regarding external things, one calculates only the characteristics of "self" and "mine"; regarding internal things, one calculates both the characteristics of "self" and "mine. (Although "self-characteristic" was indicated above, it actually encompasses both "self" and "mine").

This is because all treatises that remedy the notion of a self (*ātman*) do so by abandoning both "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*). Here, this refers specifically to external things belonging to the self). Nevertheless, within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there are three types of "what belongs to the self."

1. *Mamāyita* (that which is associated with "mine"). Because the self is associated with them, it is said that they exist; these are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (as in the expression, "I have form," and so forth).

2. *Anuvartaka-mamāyita* (that which follows from the power of "mine"). This refers to when something functions through the sovereign power of the self—whether being relinquished or employed—the world says of it, "It is mine.
These are likewise the five aggregates; because the self possesses power, form and the others belong to the self, and thus the self employs them. 3. *A-* [incomplete]...

"Detachment from 'mine' (mamakāra)" refers to such notions as "I am in form," and so forth. They conceive of a real self that dwells within the aggregates (*skandha*), following throughout the entire body.

(That is the person who conceives; this refers to the conception of a self pervading the five aggregates. The above is explained in terms of the internal. As for the external, it is as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:

to conceive of a self within the five aggregates is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Within each of the five aggregates, there are three types of "mine": first, the adornment of the self; second, the [possession] of the self...
Servants: these three were my dwellings; now they are called the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which are merely my subordinates.

Since they were previously included within "my servants" and "my possessions," by now separating from these aggregates, one is able to exercise mastery over them. As for what are called the five aggregates, they refer to the bhikṣu and the bhikṣuṇī.
Śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs—if within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, it mentions only the four assemblies (that is, the two outer and two inner assemblies;

here, referring specifically to the inner assemblies, it is called the five assemblies). Thus that sūtra says: "There are two kinds of tranquility: first, tranquility of mind; second, tranquility of body.
As for tranquility of body, it means not associating with the four assemblies and not participating in any of their affairs. As for tranquility of mind..."
One never cultivates greed, anger, or delusion. There may be those whose bodies are tranquil but whose minds are not;

this refers to a bhikṣu sitting in meditation in a quiet place, secluded from the fourfold assembly, yet whose mind constantly accumulates greed, hatred, and delusion. Or there may be those whose minds are tranquil but whose bodies are not;
this refers to a bhikṣu who associates with kings and ministers, yet has severed greed, hatred, and delusion. Or there may be those whose bodies and minds are both tranquil.

This refers to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whose minds are tranquil because they currently cultivate the contemplation of the three emptinesses, and whose bodies are tranquil because they remain distant from the five aggregates.

Alternatively, there are those whose bodies and minds are both not tranquil, namely ordinary worldlings, who are unable to deeply contemplate impermanence, non-self, and impurity. Furthermore, it is said:

"To dwell near a secluded place and remain far removed from clamor and bustle is called tranquility" (identical to the present text). According to the above scriptural passages, all define tranquility as being separated from the fourfold assembly.
"Jing" (Quietude) is entirely identical in meaning to "separation from the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*) as used here.

However, Zhuzhuo erroneously cites the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates in the *Lotus Sūtra* to prove that the five aggregates are the same as the five constituents (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), merely differing in transliteration.

He goes so far as to rebuke Guoshan for providing a literal interpretation of "disciples," yet his own exposition is recorded [in the canon]. This greatly contradicts the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and involves a reckless citation of the *Lotus Sūtra*; his erroneous critique forcibly subverts the established translations.

This is an extreme case of superficiality. (However, if one were to interpret this as representing the dharmas—using the five aggregates to represent the five skandhas—there is indeed such an ancient interpretation. How can one then explain it by equating the meaning of "accumulation" directly with the meaning of "concealment"?).

If that were so, then the four assemblies of *nirvāṇa* would have to consist of the four aggregates (*skandha*). Regarding the statement "arising in disorder without sequence": if one is attached to the five aggregates, because of the obstruction of "mine" (*mamakāra*), body and mind become confused and disordered;

thus, because the practice of contemplation lacks continuity, one is made to leave such clamor and distraction behind. Third, "the three below" refers to those two being obstacles to signlessness (*animitta*).
This applies generally to the absence of self and what belongs to self (*anātman-anātmīya*); these are not themselves obstacles, but are designated as such in relation to their respective remedies.
The objects to be remedied are as follows: just as that which is known is not itself an obstruction, yet this obstruction obstructs what is known.

Because one dwells alone, the body is tranquil; because one lives in seclusion, the mind is tranquil. Fourth, regarding "the lower": the obstructions to the primary virtues, of which the four unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) are foremost.

For a person dwelling in a quiet place who enters the three gates of emptiness, these constitute the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna and thus become the primary virtues. Therefore, they can remedy the obstructions to the primary virtues of the unconditioned.
Regarding the obstacle to virtue: because the person dwelling in a quiet place now has the contemplation of emptiness manifest before them, the gods of the Śakra-heaven revere them.
To state it fully: *Śakradevendra*. *Śakra* means "able"; *deva* means "heavenly"; *indra* means "lord. Thus, he is the "Able Lord of Heaven.
Because he nurtures beings and exhorts them toward goodness, and because he is able to act as the lord of heaven, he, along with the other hosts of devas, holds them in high esteem.
Regarding the cultivation of the lower [stages], there are two doors of cultivation for distancing oneself. First, following what preceded:

although by nature one is free from "self" and "what belongs to self," if one does not abandon the assembly, there is still fear that it will arise again. Now, since one has abandoned both one's own assembly and other assemblies, they do not arise.

Abiding in the Dharma, one regards one's own assembly as "self" and other assemblies as "what belongs to self"; this would contradict the previous treatise’s point regarding the five aggregates as obstacles consisting of "what belongs to self."
Furthermore, he has missed the essential meaning of this chapter most egregiously; yet, within his erroneous interpretation, he further disparages the former masters—how can he be so exceptional?

Since the preceding treatise already explained the sūtra’s “leaving clamor” by means of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), he now abandons his own group for another group, which refers to his own and others’ followers.
According to the intent of the previous scripture, those who seek the three emptinesses (*tri-śūnyatā*) to remedy the mark of self (*ātma-grāha*) should externally leave behind [such attachments].

For those who possess the notion of "mine," the wisdom of contemplation is quickly accomplished. Now, one must also cause them to relinquish both self and others; thus, they will no longer accumulate the notions of "I" and "mine.
Below the section on "Skillful Means and Wisdom," one welcomes the superior relinquishment of the assembly, whereby skillful means and wisdom are perfected.

One should dwell in seclusion, which constitutes dwelling in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding the section on "Thorough Discernment": although one dwells in seclusion through the aforementioned skillful means and wisdom, if one does not...

One contemplates the cessation of the root of suffering because it is not [yet] well-discriminated. Now that one has contemplated its cessation, this is called the accomplishment of well-discriminating wisdom.

It distances one from the cause of arising; that which gives rise to suffering is called the "cause of suffering. This cause is precisely the fundamental cause of that suffering, namely, the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
Since this grasping at a self and phenomena is headed by the view of a transitory collection (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), it constitutes the fundamental cause of suffering. Therefore...
In the *Vijñaptimātratā* it is said: "The grasping at a self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ātma-grāha*) all take the view of a transitory collection (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as their primary view.

When associated with afflictions such as doubt and ignorance, the suffering of the two types of death does not cease. Now, because one extinguishes the fundamental cause of suffering, it is called 'distancing' (*dūrībhāva*)."
Third, the section on the enjoyment of various views, which has three parts. Regarding "enjoying the lower": first, there is the arising of affliction through the enjoyment [of views].

As for the phrase "enjoying various views," it refers to the scriptural statement, "because one undergoes manifold afflictions. Regarding this "conceptual arising," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)..."

This refers to the grasping at the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as "self" (*ātman*) and "belonging to self" (*ātmīya*). Its function is to serve as the basis for all speculative views (*dṛṣṭi-gata*).

(This is identical to the current treatise’s discussion on the arising of "self" and "belonging to self" from oneself and others; "grasping" is precisely the accumulation of craving). There are twenty phrases of differentiation within these views, which constitute the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*).
The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "That is to say, as it is conceived: 'Form is the self,' 'I possess form,' 'Form belongs to me,' or 'I am in [form]...'"
Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa*), one aggregate consists of four [aspects], and thus the five aggregates together comprise twenty. Five of these constitute the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);

the remainder are all "mine" (*mama*). These are: the "associated mine" (i.e., "I have form"), the "concomitant mine" (i.e., "form belongs to me"), and the "inseparable mine" (i.e., "I am within form").
Thus, there are fifteen instances of "mine. This is the analysis of the formations that take the aggregates as their object, and it is also the analysis of the basis from which they arise.
All of these are conceptualizations of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). If one enumerates them across the three periods of time, there are sixty;

adding "the body is the self" makes sixty-one, and "the self is distinct from the body" makes sixty-two. These are the sixty-two views that arise based on the view of a self in the body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the sutra’s reference to "delighting in the assembly and undergoing affliction": the "assembly" refers to the objective environment (*viṣaya*), and the "delight" refers to the mind.

Because the mind delights in the assembly, one gives rise to views of "I" and "mine," which is termed "undergoing the affliction of the assembly. Regarding the passage "all views, once arisen, harm themselves": when various views accumulate in the mind, one sinks into ruin;
just as when many birds gather on a tree, it withers and breaks. Furthermore, regarding the passage "it further demonstrates... [the third point is] non-existence.
The characteristic of renunciation: because afflictions, karma, and birth immediately give rise to suffering, one sinks into suffering due to the bondage of views;
this can be understood through both the teaching and its analogy.

third, the commentary and explanation, which has two parts. First, diligence, which has two parts. First, the explanation according to the Dharma (dharmadeśanā). The commentary says, below...

Answer: There are two reasons. First, the foundations of mindfulness are among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
