This is the meaning. Furthermore, the foundations of mindfulness are the basis for the arising of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) of a Tathāgata; therefore, when one regresses from them, it is said that one has regressed from the knowledge of all aspects of a Tathāgata

At the very beginning, this is the foremost of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). If one repeatedly neglects the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), then all practices will be lost; therefore, only this is mentioned.
In the analogy, it refers to ceasing before [the fire] has heated up, because it is close to the heat of the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);

thus, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*)—which is the stage of application (*prayoga*)—is indicated here by the phrase "not yet heated. Within the stage of Provisions (*sambhāra*), one first cultivates the general and specific foundations of mindfulness; having already regressed from them...

Then all other practices would be lost. Second, the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are common to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; they remedy the eight inversions, such as permanence and impermanence.
Furthermore, by deeply contemplating the foundations of mindfulness, one immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);

therefore, if these are lost, all else fails to be accomplished. It is for this reason alone that [the text] refers specifically to them. (Regarding the term "abiding in the Dharma": it may refer to whatever dharmas are received by ordinary beings, such as the three trainings and the eightfold path; whatever is practiced accordingly is called a foundation of mindfulness. This groundless talk originates from mere personal fancy.)

The third [section] concerns the merit of the five kinds of non-forgetfulness. First, the heading is presented: "non-forgetfulness" is equivalent to "right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*), because forgetfulness is precisely "erroneous thought" (*mithyā-manasikāra*).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* simply states: "The sixth is right mindfulness. That sutra clarifies the sequence, saying:

"This diligent practitioner binds the mind to six points—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, generosity, and the devas. This is called right mindfulness" (furthermore, it possesses the four foundations of mindfulness).

The state is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Furthermore, the cultivation of the Great Nirvāṇa is called right mindfulness. Moreover, to apply the mind in contemplation that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and subject to no change is called right mindfulness. Now, it is by means of diligence that [this is achieved].
"Constantly not forgetting mindfulness" is the foremost of all practices; therefore, it follows next. Second, citing the sutra; third, the commentary’s explanation, which has two parts.
Regarding the section beginning with "The commentary says," the first part indicates two meanings, which are then explained in the subsequent section.
Second, the detailed explanation of the two meanings has two parts. Regarding the first, "Among these... and so forth: first, the explanation of being the foremost of all formations (*saṃskāra*).

In reality, all formations have non-forgetfulness (*asmṛti*) as their foremost; however, this sutra speaks briefly, referring to it simply as the head of the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
This is easily seen from the text. Regarding the second, "It can obstruct... and so forth: the second explanation is that it can destroy the heavy enmity since beginningless time. That is to say—

Taking the three unwholesome roots—greed and the others—as one’s heavy enemies from time immemorial, if one does not now forget mindfulness, one can ward off these heavy enemies and prevent them from harming the three wholesome roots.

(Regarding the "abiding in the Dharma": because the three wholesome roots are powerful, the enemies cannot harm them; this means the three wholesome roots ward off the heavy enemies. It is not that mindfulness alone can ward them off; [otherwise] you would contradict the treatise.

In the previous section, guarding the wholesome was discussed; here, warding off the unwholesome is discussed. In both cases, it is non-forgetfulness of mindfulness that is the foremost among all practices. Regarding...
The principle becomes even clearer. Regarding the term "afflictions" (*kleśa*) below, this is a specific explanation of the character "entering" (*praveśa*) in the Sūtra.

That is to say, for one who is forgetful, the internal mind is deluded and disturbed; thus, afflictions enter therein. Furthermore, because of this disturbance, external conditions gather to produce faults;

this is what is meant by "the thief entering. Now, because of non-forgetfulness, the internal mind is not disturbed; therefore, afflictions do not enter the mind, which renders external thieves unable [to cause harm].

This collects and gives rise to faults. These "affliction-thieves" (kleśa-caura) are a metaphor for the three unwholesome roots (akuśala-mūla). This is merely a matter of internal disturbance and external accumulation;
when mind and object correspond, the three unwholesome [roots] arise. As for the established doctrine, afflictions are delusions (moha), while "thieves" specifically metaphorize karma (*karman*).

According to the *Abhidharma-kośa*, they are called "deadly enemies" because they harm the three wholesome roots. Since they thus destroy the three wholesome roots, it is certain that the affliction-thieves metaphorize the three unwholesome [roots].
This is the root. Second, the exhortation to cultivate and achieve virtue has two parts. "Furthermore, [the passage] below" indicates the first part, the exhortation to practice.

Regarding the statement, "Now, those who achieve success in the initial and final moments of thought," this explains the sūtra’s injunction that one should always maintain mindfulness within the mind; thus, one achieves success in the initial and final moments of thought. (This is the Zang edition. If the Lingzhi edition says, "causing the initial thought... [it continues as follows].)

Regarding the phrase "accomplishment in the locus" (*sthāna-siddhi*): the character *chù* (locus) is an error; for the sake of the meaning, the subsequent character [of the commentary] should be used as correct. The *Zhǔfǎ shì* (Commentary on the Abiding Dharma) states: "This refers to the period before the event has actually arrived. This explains that one should constantly collect the mind within the heart (*citta*). One does not know what [the author] was referring to [by this].

Moreover, how could there be any connection between this and the subsequent explanation of the "beginningless mind"? As for the statement, "It is said to manifest [this] in order to exclude the beginningless mind": since the sutra already instructs one to "constantly collect the mind within the heart," we can verify from this that it excludes [the notion of] a "beginningless mind.

The "beginning mind" is simply the "initial mind. If even the subsequent thoughts of the present can be accomplished, how much more so [can the initial mind]? How could there be anything that lacks a beginning?

Is it the initial mind? Therefore, it is said that "it obstructs you. Regarding the phrase "abiding in the dharma," two interpretations are provided; both explain the word "mind" (*citta*) by reference to the beginningless.

How much error is there [in this]? As for the statement regarding the "loss of the beginning and end": above, it was based on the accomplishment of the first and last moments, whereby there is the attainment of the beginning and end of those moments;
therefore, here is the loss of the beginning and end of those moments. This explains the sūtra’s "if one loses mindfulness."
This refers to losing mindfulness from beginning to end. To say that one "accomplishes many faults" explains that, according to the sutra, one thereby loses all merits.

This means one loses all the aforementioned practices as well as the three roots of goodness. Furthermore, to accomplish the latter two accomplishments of virtue is to accomplish the virtue of benefiting others.
As for the preceding merit of seclusion, it causes one to abandon the multitude and dwell alone; this accords with the world, even though—
Entering into the five desires, one still does not forget mindfulness; there are two meanings for this distinction. First, it is according to the sequence of the text:
because of contentment, one distances oneself; because of distancing oneself, one exerts diligence; because of exerting diligence, one does not forget mindfulness.

Among these, for one whose power of mindfulness is strong, even if they employ the means of "gathering beings through shared activities," this actually serves as a counter-illustration that such a person of strong mindfulness should not act in that way. The text possesses a sequential order to reveal this.

The meanings are not identical; they should not be treated as one standard. Second, they differ in their function as gateways: the former is wisdom (*jñāna*) and this is compassion (*karuṇā*), for these two meanings are distinct.
This accords with the worldly accumulation of merit through altruistic practice. The analogy and its application may be understood accordingly.

The third section concerns the merits of the six dhyānas. First, the heading is presented. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The samādhi attained by one who possesses right mindfulness is right concentration.
This sutra itself says: "If one collects the mind, the mind is then in concentration. Therefore, this follows next.
Second, citing the sutra; third, the commentary explaining it in three parts. First, showing the cause and function of concentration. First, the cause of concentration, which comprises mindfulness.

The commentary says, "First, the explicit explanation": regarding the term "eight dhyāna-concentrations," if one distinguishes their characteristics, the term "dhyāna" applies generally to all eight as they are called "concentration," yet only the first four are specifically named "dhyāna.
Now, when we speak of the "eight kinds of dhyāna-concentration," it should be understood as the four dhyānas and the [four formless concentrations].
Concentration (*samādhi*). It is said to be accomplished in eight types, all of which are meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). If one explains the etymology, it should follow its specific designation.

Regarding the term "four dhyānas" (*catur-dhyāna*), the full expression is *dhyāna*. The correct term is *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and discernment). [In ancient translations,] "contemplation-cultivation" (*sīwéixiū*), "grove of merit" (*gōngdé cónglín*), and "abandoning" (*qì*) were all semantic translations;

the correct term is *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. "Śama" means tranquility; "vipaśyanā" means analytical investigation. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "With respect to the object of focus, one binds the mindfulness in tranquil stillness..."

Because it involves both contemplation (*cintā*) and reflection (*dhyāna*), it is called *dhyāna*. Thus, through stillness (*śamatha*), one can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and through reflection (*vipaśyanā*), one can engage in correct observation.

In the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there is stillness but no reflection; although they can sever the fetters, they cannot provide correct observation. In the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the desire realm, there is reflection but no stillness.

Although one may practice correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), one cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, only those within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) alone receive this name. Regarding the "four concentrations of emptiness" (*catasraḥ śūnyatā-samāpattayaḥ*):

"emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to the Formless (*ārūpya*), and "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), meaning causing the mind to focus exclusively on a single object.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Within these four stages, because all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) have been transcended (meaning that the qualities of the stage are predominant), they oppose and harm [the realm of form]."
Because all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) [are absent]—that is, because harmful material phenomena cannot possibly arise there—it is like a flower in the sky.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that they are "formless" (*ārūpya*). However, the Mahāsāṃghika and Mahīśāsaka schools also maintain that there is form;

it is called "non-existent" because it is subtle. Thus, all four are collectively termed "empty" (*śūnya*). (The above explains the collective name. As for the individual explanation of the four dhyānas: the first has applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
The dhyānas with applied and sustained thought; second, the dhyāna without applied or sustained thought; third, the dhyāna free from joy; and fourth, the dhyāna free from bliss (referring to:

first dhyāna, which is free from sensual desires and evil while possessing applied and sustained thought; second dhyāna, which lacks applied and sustained thought but possesses joy and bliss; third dhyāna, which is free from the movement of joy and possesses the sensation of bliss; and fourth dhyāna, which is free from the sensation of bliss, thus characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness). As for the distinctions among the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*):

first, the concentration on the sphere of infinite space (referring to contemplating space, forming the mental aspect of "infinite," being able to extinguish the perception of form, and resting the mind in the concentration of space); second, the [sphere of infinite] consciousness...

1. The Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*): This refers to the mind taking internal consciousness as its object and forming the mental aspect of "infinite. It serves as an antidote to the contemplation of emptiness regarding lower realms and to the coarse discrimination of external thoughts;

thus, one settles the mind in concentration upon consciousness. 2. The Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*): This refers to the absence of both the internal and the external. That is, one contemplates the aforementioned relinquishing of external objects and the coarseness and floating nature of internal mental events. Consequently, there is no grasping; since the grasped (*grāhya*) is absent, the grasper (*grāhaka*) is also absent. Thus, there is neither internal nor external. 3. The Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*):

This means that because the clear perceptions of the lower realms are absent, it is called "without perception" (*asaṃjñā*). Because there is occasionally a subtle, inferior perception, it is called "not non-perception" (*na-asaṃjñā*). [The remainder of the passage is omitted].

[The practitioner] uses this to treat all previous perceptions (*saṃjñā*). These, moreover, are coarse conceptualizations and discriminations. The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "First, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), thereby transcending all perceptions of existence. Now, one further transcends the perception of nothingness; therefore, it is called 'neither-perception' (*na-saṃjñā*). Furthermore, regarding the term "neither-non-perception" (*na-vi-saṃjñā*):

it is not like the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), wherein all perceptions are entirely extinguished. Here, there remains only a subtle perception. Outsiders do not understand this and mistake it for *nirvāṇa*. Since they have not yet attained objectlessness (*anālambana*), how could they be free from the mind and its objects?

Moreover, they reckon this state as a self and subsequently give rise to attachment to its flavor. If one recognizes these faults, one seeks further advancement. When seeking further advancement, one seeks an object of focus above that, but realizes that nothing can be apprehended (*anupalabdhi*). Because nothing is apprehended, [the mind] ceases and does not revolve; thus, one attains cessation (*nirodha*).

The attainment of the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*). If one has not yet attained this meditative absorption, one first develops a distaste for perception; subsequently, as perception no longer functions, one enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). If one is a disciple of the Buddha, within these very attainments, one advances toward and realizes the truly untainted (*anāsrava*) state. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

The names of the three [formless attainments], beginning with "Infinite Space," are established based on their preparatory practices (*prayoga*). The name "Neither Perception nor Non-perception" is established because it is dull and inferior.

This means that during the stage of preparatory practice prior to cultivating the concentration, because one has become weary of and overcome form (*rūpa*), one forms a resolute perception (*adhimokṣa-saṃjñā*) and contemplates the infinite...

Regarding the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*): when the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is perfected, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. One becomes weary of the perception of space and perceives consciousness; one becomes weary of the perception of consciousness and perceives nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*). This should be understood by analogy.

As for the fourth sphere, because its perception is dull and inferior—meaning it lacks the superior perception of clear wisdom found in the lower stages—it receives the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Because there remains a dull and inferior perception, it is named "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. Thus, the names of the preceding [three] are derived from their preparatory applications, while the fourth is named from its preparatory application.

Because their fundamental practice shares the same object of focus, they should be designated by their essential nature. Regarding the eight higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), there is no divergence between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools.

In the Hīnayāna, one practices by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); yet, if one returns to the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), then all the factors and branches of the eight attainments are entirely empty.
When phenomena are exhausted and principle manifests, everything is the *tathāgatagarbha*. When all distinctions have ceased and there is nowhere to rely, then both concentration and distraction—
[This is] lost. If phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, then one is all. Since this scriptural passage concerns the Mahāyāna, it is not that it does not accord with emptiness;

however, it speaks in terms of conventional characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to universally guide those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The term "etc. (*ādi*) refers to all other meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
All of these arise from one another. The *Dui-zhi* (Treatise on Antidotes) states: "Among the four dhyānas, there are distinctions in samādhi."

There are immeasurable names, beyond calculation. Among the samādhis included within the first dhyāna, even all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot comprehend the names of the samādhis entered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, let alone know their number, much less realize and enter them.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is with the samādhis included within the remaining dhyānas and the formless realms.
Thus, by means of the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one equalizes all things.

As for the phrase "How [is this] below?", this is a double interrogation and explanation. That is to say, although it was previously stated that mindfulness is gathered, the specific mode of activity (*ākāra*) was not yet known; therefore, this interrogation and explanation follows.

Here, "gathering" refers to the antidote, while "mental activity" (*citta-saṃskāra*) refers to that which is to be countered. "Object" (*ālambana*) refers to the mind that takes an object, and "place" (*sthāna*) refers to the locus.
Regarding the objects upon which these mental activities depend: among them, mental activities are fundamentally of three grades—superior, intermediate, and inferior.
Since the intermediate and inferior grades are identical in their engagement with objects, they are combined into one; thus, there are only two kinds of objective spheres.

Within the superior grade of mental activity, what is called "mental activity that pervades all spheres of operation" refers to the predominance of the distracted mind within the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states.

It pervades all locations throughout the three realms and universally takes the three periods of time as its objects; thus, it is the universal range of this mental activity. Regarding the term "mental activity" (*citta-carita*):

it refers to the nature of flux and volitional construction. (The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* explains the meaning of "universal" [sarvatraga] as follows: "Universal across time," because it functions universally throughout the three periods of time; "universal across realms," because it pervades the three realms.

Furthermore, in the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*, the universal factors are explained as being "universal by way of nature, stage, and time. Here, "nature" refers to the three natures; "stage" refers to the nine stages; "time" refers to the same time; and "concomitance" refers to their coexistence with the eight consciousnesses). Regarding the term "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*):
Regarding the term "condition" (*pratyaya*): it now precisely subsumes this mind of objective consideration; thus, it is called the "counteractive condition.

As for the phrase "next, and below," the character "subsume" (*saṃgraha*) from above runs through the meaning. To say "subsume the soft within" means to take up the mental activities regarding phenomena.

"Middle" refers to the middle-grade mind, and "soft" refers to the lower-grade mind. "Soft" refers to the lower-grade mind, as the various treatises of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna explain the superior [grades].
"Medium and inferior. It is mostly said that these are "superior, medium, and soft. The *Qingliang shi* (Commentary by Qingliang) states: "Soft" means inferior.

This is because at the initial moment of grasping an object, the mind is still light and soft; thus, it is designated as "soft" by way of its inferior grade. These all take present objects as their domain, which is why they are called "grasping objects" (*shou-shi*).

They differ from the superior grade of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), which can take past and future objects as their conditions. The character "comprehending" (*she*) serves as the antidote to this discursive cogitation; hence, it is said to "counteract" (*dui*).
This refers to the objects of focus for cultivation. Thus, the conclusion states: "These two kinds of focal points" refer to the focal points for the two kinds of mental activities.

When one cultivates these so that the mind is not distracted, it is called the time of accomplishment; therefore, one draws near to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This concerns the errors regarding the abiding in the Dharma.

To claim that because [the afflictions] are seen to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are therefore weak among the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga*)—this is groundless talk resulting from the fault of not having closely studied the sūtras and śāstras.

Below the section on meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*): The two functions are accomplished by means of concentration; wisdom is generated because of concentration, and wisdom is precisely the functional fruit.

Thus, one is able to know the arising and ceasing of the world and so forth. By entering meditative concentration, this is called the "worldly path" (*laukika-mārga*) within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Therefore...

Within this, one knows the arising and ceasing of the world. This is the "raising of the jade. It refers to the subtle habitual tendencies that arise and cease within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which obstruct the dhyānas and other states. This is it.

Second, clarifying the diligent cultivation that remedies indolence. Furthermore, "the laxity below" [refers to] the first part, which provides a general summary. The Sūtra admonishes constant diligence and recognizes that immobility is an obstacle;
it is because one does not know the skillful means of cultivation that one becomes indolent. Below, the three types of indolence are clarified.

That is, the obstacle to skillful means (*upāya*) is laziness (*kausīdya*). Because this laziness obstructs skillful means, and because skillful means consists precisely of the three remedial methods such as moderation in food (*mātrajñatā*) and so forth.
Second, the detailed explanation of these two [obstacles and remedies] follows. Within this, first is the laziness that is the object to be remedied;

these three are collectively termed obstacles to skillful means. Next is the section on the reconciliation of the explanation. "How so? introduces the second part: diligence (*vīrya*), which is the remedy. First, the inquiry; then, "Manifesting... and so forth.
Commentary: First, regarding the treatment of instability: regulating the quantity of food and sleep treats the instability of the body;

practicing *ānāpāna* (here translated as "sending forth and sending back," or alternatively "exhalation and inhalation"—this *ānāpānasmṛti* is as explained elsewhere and is not recorded here in detail) treats the instability of the mind.

Second, regarding the treatment of lack of flavor: "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers generally to the supernormal faculties; "wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to discerning wisdom; "merit" (*guṇa*) applies to both; and "exhausting the source of suffering" refers to the exhaustion of the origin of duḥkha.
This is liberation. Because it possesses the three aforementioned qualities, it is called a "great and marvelous matter. Regarding the third point, the treatment of terrors:

among birth, aging, sickness, and death, these occur most frequently among humans. As for the four evil destinies—namely, ghosts, hells, animals, and asuras—one should practice the contemplation that all five destinies are suffering.
The reason the heavens are not mentioned is that their characteristics of suffering are subtle; they are not so terrifying as to readily inspire the exertion of diligent effort.
It is omitted and not mentioned.
These are the three lower fetters (*saṃyojana*). Regarding the two [stages] of the fixed merit (*niyata-guṇa*), one further cultivates the first dharma of the lower [stage].

Because the mind is not distracted, it is called "having nothing to be counteracted" (*apratipakṣa*). From this, it is verified that by means of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for the objects of the two higher types, one attains proximity to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

This refers to gathering the distracted mind. Furthermore, there are two metaphors below: if the mind is distracted, one not only fails to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), but also loses wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, the pond is a metaphor for concentration, and the water is a metaphor for wisdom. Now, because the mind is not distracted, [the water remains].
It is not only that meditative concentration is accomplished, but wisdom is also brought forth;

therefore, it is called "superior and superior increase. Section Seven: The Merit of Wisdom (in three parts). First, the heading of the chapter: Previously, it was said that one cultivates dhyāna for the sake of the water of wisdom;

now, the purpose [of this cultivation] is clarified, which is why it follows next. Second, citing the sutra. Third, the commentary’s explanation (in four parts). First, clarifying the obstacles and their remedies. The treatise says:

Below: First, the explicit clarification. The first phrase cites the chapter title. From "Regarding the true" (*zhēn*) onwards: second, the formal explanation. The "locus of the true meaning" (*zhēnshí yìchù*) refers to the sphere of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
this is that which is obstructed. That "clinging" (*tānzhù*) is the obstructor. The "locus of worldly affairs" (*shìjiān shìchù*) is likewise that which is obstructed.
Furthermore, attachment is also identified as an obstacle; in both cases, the object is cited to indicate the subject.
Regarding these two obstacles, that which is able to distance itself from them is what the Sūtra refers to as "wisdom. Since there are two obstacles, wisdom is likewise divided into two.

In relation to the first obstacle, it is the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which can counteract the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding the principle and illuminates the sphere of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In relation to the subsequent obstacle...

This is precisely the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which remedies the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding phenomena and illuminates the objects of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, the first hindrance is the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the subsequent hindrance is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);

it is also termed the "obscuration of principle" (*tattvāvaraṇa*) and the "obscuration of phenomena" (*vastvāvaraṇa*). These latent tendencies that delude one regarding principle and phenomena are the seeds of the two obscurations; thus, they constitute both the subject and object of the hindrances.

Each of these is divided into two meanings. Among them, greed (*lobha*) is the head of both the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). By citing the first, the subsequent ones are indicated; therefore, the Sūtra mentions only greed.

Nevertheless, the essence of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) consists of the same afflictions, such as greed; they are distinguished as two different obstructions only by way of their obstructing the principle (*li*) or the phenomena (*shi*).
Thus, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, regarding both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is taken as the basis.
Taking [ignorance] as the primary [cause], it extends to all afflictions (*kleśa*). These two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are distinguished solely by their obstruction of *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*.
The present case is likewise; thus, Qingliang said: "The cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also takes the afflictions as its obstructing agent. This is precisely that meaning.
Now, it is clarified that because one possesses wisdom and is free from greed, one is able to distance oneself from both obstacles. Regarding the first point below:
Second is the exhortation to practice. The treatise explains two phrases of the sūtra with two phrases. Regarding the statement therein that it is "difficult to obtain":
this wisdom can sever both obstacles simultaneously, and because it is extremely difficult to obtain, one must not allow it to be lost.
"Furthermore, it is shown below. Second, regarding the ability to obtain benefit: the previous statement "difficult to obtain" refers in meaning to both obstacles.
Now, regarding the phrase "difficult to obtain yet able to obtain," it simply says "far removed from the sphere of the ultimate truth" because, within my Dharma, one is able to attain liberation.

One is liberated within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that one "remains far removed from the ultimate reality" (the aforementioned "true reality" is precisely this "ultimate reality").

This refers to the time when the practitioner first enters into realization: first, they give rise to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) which takes the realm of true reality (*satya-dharmatā*) as its object;

hence, it is said "in the ultimate reality. Furthermore, because one is able to simultaneously sever both types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—those deluded regarding principle and those deluded regarding phenomena—it is said:
"Detachment. This explains that within the Tathāgata’s ultimate (paramārtha) dharma, one attains liberation by severing both obstacles simultaneously;
thus it is called detachment. (This meaning is explained at length in the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, citing the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

As for the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which arises subsequent to the fundamental [wisdom], it exclusively and separately illuminates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and separately severs the delusions regarding phenomena; therefore, it is not mentioned here. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "To realize..."
The meaning is that conventional [knowledge] is called "subsequently attained" because it arises from realizing the ultimate truth; this is precisely what is intended.

Although the *Zhufa ji* (Record of the Abiding Dharma) contains profound intent, its interpretation of the text is not clear, for it states that "it is far removed from the sphere of the primary meaning," thereby implying that it exists within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding liberation through the removal of obstructions, when has it ever been said that even the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is to be discarded?

Therefore, what was stated previously—that there are "obstructions regarding the state of reality"—and what is stated now—that one is "free from [obstructions] regarding the state of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha*)—the meaning is perfectly clear. Why resort to such forced interpretation?

Furthermore, the text below shows this by repeating the refutation three times. "Intrinsic wisdom" (*svabhāva-prajñā*) refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), also called the wisdom of the true essence (*samyak-svabhāva-jñāna*).

This wisdom transcends the world; since the present case does not involve this wisdom, one cannot be called a person who has transcended the world. Nevertheless, he has already left the household life.
Furthermore, it does not constitute a worldly layperson; thus, it resembles neither of the two. However, "monk" and "layperson" are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Since this is neither of these two names, it is said to be "not a designation."
The four similes illustrate two types of merit. Furthermore, from "below" [the text], the first is the primary simile. The *Zhufa ji* states:

Hearing the Dharma and attaining awakening leads to transcendence of birth and death, like a boat crossing the sea; contemplating and observing can shatter ignorance, like a lamp illuminating darkness;

practicing to eliminate karma is like medicine curing disease; realizing the principle and severing delusions is like an axe felling a tree. The sea is a metaphor for the path of suffering, and disease...

The karmic path is illustrated by the metaphor of darkness and the tree, while the path of afflictions is illustrated by the two [preceding factors]. This is because the second [type of] wisdom—wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)—is the wisdom of inference prior to the [supramundane] path, which, like a lamp dispelling darkness, eliminates the obscurations.

The fourth is realized wisdom (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*). It is like an axe felling a tree: when darkness is dispelled, a lamp returns to darkness; but once a tree is felled, it will never grow again. Because the objects eliminated by these two types of realization differ, two metaphors are employed.

Thus, four dharmas are used to counteract the three paths. What the Sūtra calls "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and what the Śāstra calls "realization" (*pratisaṃvid*) mutually clarify the agent and the object, making the meaning even more evident (the preceding coarse script is all from that text).
As for the term "actual wisdom," it refers merely to the actual capacity, as in the case of a metaphorical antidote; it does not mean [direct] realization.

Regarding the wisdom of reality (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*): because it is established through the comparative realization of the four wisdoms as being distinct, one explains the sūtra within the context of these four and thereby increases [the understanding] for oneself;
that is to say, the four qualities are successively augmented until the fourth, which is most excellent.

Second, "Furthermore, below the four" [refers to] the second [section], which reveals the merits. Regarding the phrase "within the internal spheres": this refers to the internal eye-sphere (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
Because the fleshly eye has obstructions and does not perceive forms beyond barriers, it is called "within the internal spheres.

Now, within these very internal spheres, one attains the functional utility of the four merits of illumination and awareness (the "abiding in the Dharma" means taking the internal spheres as the stage of ordinary beings). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that the Bodhisattva...
When practicing *prajñā*, one attains the five eyes. Because the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is purified, one is able to see the trichiliocosm.
This also clarifies that the wisdom of *prajñā* possesses the function of illuminating and awakening.
Regarding the eighth, "Ultimate Merit," there are two parts. Having already explained the preceding stages, this first section serves as a general conclusion and heading for what follows.

Previously, it was generally indicated that one "prolongs the difficult-to-accomplish skillful means" and "reaches the ultimate. This is because through the seven preceding stages, one gradually nurtures [the faculties] until they reach fulfillment in the eighth.
In those seven, each preceding stage gives rise to each succeeding one, thereby nurturing the conditions; now, at this point, they are finally brought to completion.
Therefore, the first seven stages are clarified in their sequential order, while the eighth stage universally builds upon those preceding seven.

Furthermore, the first seven are combined to constitute the eighth as a preparatory skillful means (*upāya*), because the eighth involves the ultimate entry into realization. Now, [the eighth] universally builds upon the first seven as a nourishing skillful means.
The arising of the eighth is called the "accomplishment of the ultimate. This refers to the practitioner’s sequential skillful means;

through liberation, the ultimate accomplishment of self-awakening is achieved. Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the latter two [stages] praise liberation, as well as the transformational birth in nirvāṇa, which pertains to benefiting others through compassion.
Regarding the abiding in the Dharma: the first five are the skillful means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while the sixth is the correct [path].
Cultivation. Seventh, wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the preceding seven are the causes, and the eighth is the fruit. The commentary states:

By citing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* for each successive stage above, it clarifies the order of their arising; this sufficiently demonstrates that it is not merely the case that the first seven are the causes and the eighth is the fruit, but that this applies universally to all.
Second, the detailed explanation based on the citation is divided into two parts. First, the citation of the sutra; second, the commentary’s explanation, which has three sections.

First, the distinction between the cultivated and the innate nature. The commentary states [from the section] "First, a general clarification of the intent": the first phrase follows the topical outline. *Nirvāṇa* is called liberation (*vimukti*). This sutra is titled "Non-discursive Elaboration" (*aprapañca*).
Liberation directly clarifies that which is abandoned; here, by contrast, it reveals that which is abandoned. Although it is revealed through contrast, it does not directly cite [the term].

The same applies to both, as they are equally established as ultimate; thus the treatise makes this classification. This refers precisely to the "bliss of quiescence" mentioned in the Sūtra, and therefore it is presented here in a general sense.
The intended meaning is that it demonstrates the remoteness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vivikta*); by means of this liberation, its essence is not a remedial dharma (*pratipakṣa-dharma*).
It awaits ultimate completion; therefore, it is said that this is not an antidotal dharma.
Second, the detailed explanation has two parts. Regarding the four types [of distinctions] below: first, the sequential clarification of cultivation.

"The wisdom of the distinctions among the four characteristics" refers to the exposition by way of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) within the context of existence, non-existence, identity, difference, and so forth (1. existence, 2. non-existence, 3. both, 4. neither). The four propositions regarding identity and difference are likewise applied equally to the ultimate and conventional truths.

Emptiness and existence: all phenomena involving dualistic opposition may be analyzed through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). While the "abiding phenomenon" refers merely to emptiness and existence, the fourfold distinctions that manifest different types of wisdom are called "differentiated wisdom.
This is what constitutes the obstruction; it refers to the presence of qualities that involve dependence. Regarding the phrase "discrimination of obstructive phenomena":

if one grasps each of these four types of differentiated wisdom and its qualities as being distinct and separate, this is precisely the discrimination of obstructive phenomena. Because [one] distinguishes...
To cling to existence is the superimposition (samāropa) of false attribution; to cling to non-existence is the deprecation (apavāda) of denial. To cling to both is the contradiction of conflict;
to cling to neither is the conceptual proliferation (prapañca) of idle discourse. Thus, clinging to these individually constitutes error, whereas comprehending them collectively constitutes wisdom.

Nevertheless, although understanding and delusion differ, as long as their mutual opposition has not been forgotten, they can all be discerned. Therefore, the second line says: "Because it is discernible," which refers precisely to conceptual proliferation.

Treatise: (If the four phrases were explained individually, only the fourth phrase would constitute conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). However, here we discuss them in contrast to understanding and delusion; therefore, they are collectively termed "various kinds of conceptual proliferation. This is because within the dharma of self-nature liberation, there fundamentally exists no dharma of opposition between understanding and delusion.)

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Conceptual proliferation destroys the eye of wisdom; thus, none of these see the Buddha. Qingliang [Fazang] says: "The moment the mind arises, it immediately becomes conceptual proliferation. This is precisely that meaning. Thus, these constitute the first two lines.

The commentary on the sutra title explains that "various conceptual proliferations" (*prapañca*) are so called because they can be differentiated; this constitutes one phrase. To explain their nature is to cause the mind to become distracted.

This refers to the objective realm of discriminating wisdom (*viveka-jñāna*), wherein there are characteristics that are mutually opposed and relative. Collectively, these are termed "distracted mental proliferation. Therefore, what follows below refers to the characteristics of those merits (the phrase "abiding in the Dharma" [is included here];

in this context, the breaking of the sentence and the phrasing are entirely unintelligible). Regarding the section "Cultivating the Path" (*bhāvanā-mārga*) below: the two [subsections] serve as a negative illustration (*paryudāsa*) to reveal the wisdom of the path of cultivation regarding the fundamental nature.
The four kinds of differentiated wisdom mentioned above, as long as they involve dualistic opposition and have not yet been forgotten, are collectively termed *prapañca* (conceptual proliferation).

Therefore, the Sūtra says, "one has not yet attained liberation. This means that although these are the wisdoms of one who has left the household life to cultivate the Path, they still abide within *prapañca*; hence the word "yet" (*yǒu*).

By contrast, it is shown that only when [wisdom] is non-conceptual by its very nature (*svabhāva*) is it called liberation; thus it is said to be "not of the nature [of conceptualization]. (Liberation within *nirvāṇa* is precisely this implied contrast.)
The nature attains liberation. (This section on "abiding in the Dharma" is also deluded).
Second, the exhortation to practice distancing has two parts. "The remainder below" refers to the first part, which provides a general heading. Second, the specific explanation has two parts.

First, regarding the initial section, it clarifies that there is "distancing through cultivation with opposition," whereby one uses discriminative wisdom to overturn the four types of slander against the obstructing dharmas, thereby establishing each respective [realization].
Virtues constitute the characteristic of being subject to opposition (*sapratigha*). Since these very characteristics of opposition inevitably disturb the mind, they are said to be "far removed.
The various virtues mentioned there merely serve to explain the aforementioned characteristic of opposition; therefore, the Sūtra exhorts one to "swiftly abandon them" and so forth. Question:
The characteristics of virtue are not things that ought to be abandoned; why, then, are they also to be "far removed"? Answer: It is simply that one removes the disease, not the medicine.
This excludes that [dualistic] dharma; therefore, the sutra merely says to "urgently leave behind the distracted mind," which means to sweep away the mind of relative opposition.
Furthermore, this section precisely reveals the self-nature (*svabhāva*) in order to cause one to leave behind the mind that depends on conditions;

its intent is to reveal by contrast the subsequent section’s theme of the quiescence of self-nature (the errors regarding the abiding dharma need not be further clarified). Second, the following two points clarify non-opposition and detachment by way of nature, correctly elucidating [the point].
It is the ultimate merit of being naturally detached from self-nature. Because the bliss of quiescence is itself the self-nature of Great Nirvāṇa, the Sūtra says:
"When birth and death have ceased, quiescence is bliss. This is the sole, uniform equality, wherein the path of names and words is severed.
When the sphere of mental activity ceases, one’s own nature is naturally free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, the sutra instructs that it must be swiftly extinguished.

This serves as a reductio ad absurdum to show that any movement of the mind constitutes a deviation; only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that transcends all dependence is truly free from conceptual proliferation. Regarding the "Abiding in the Dharma," the Preface to the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"He has already entered *nirvāṇa*; all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) have been extinguished"—this is its intended meaning.

Regarding "manifestation" and below: the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are distinct. As for "the accomplishment of practice," it means that because one practices with the eight applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one achieves this [state].

Regarding "distinct essential natures," it means that by virtue of this, one does not engage in conceptual proliferation and thereby attains the fruit of liberation, which is the bliss of tranquility (*śānti*).

Therefore, it is said that its essential nature differs from that of the preceding causal practice. Furthermore, the names of the seven preceding fetters are easy to discern, so they are not explained individually;
by contrast, their quiescent essence is difficult to clarify, which is why it alone is explained here.

IV. The Section Displaying the Ultimate Profound Merits, divided into two parts. Regarding the phrase "Having already explained... and so forth: first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent one.

Here, the conclusion of the preceding section corresponds to the initial topical division of the treatise, both of which speak of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). If the eight types of awakening (*bodha*) mentioned previously were intended, why then is it said "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) here?

The answer is: because by awakening to the seven preceding skillful means (*upāya*), one nurtures the causal conditions; thus, the underlying intent lies in accomplishment, and this is how the topical division is established.

Because it indicates the general meaning, the beginning and end simply state "accomplishment. As for the sequence of the eight awakenings, although the cultivation and realization differ, this section specifically admonishes cultivation as the means to achieve them;

therefore, the heading of the text simply says "cultivation and practice. Furthermore, while the preceding portion of this middle section—relying on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—has already concluded its presentation of merits that accord with the capacities of beings, this [present] section now reveals the profoundly deep merits.
Because it accords with principle, is constantly taught, and is constantly practiced, it follows next.

Second, citing the sutra and providing an exegesis, which has two parts: first, citing the sutra; second, the treatise’s explanation, which has two parts. First, the exposition of the meaning, beginning with "The Treatise says," and so forth.

The first part is the statement of the meaning. In the commentary, beginning with "Next," the first section states the meaning. The first phrase cites the topical outline (*uddāna*); the second phrase indicates the meaning.
Within the citation, the two characters "merit" (*guṇa*)—the text for which appears below while the intent anticipates what follows above—refer to ultimate merit and profound merit.

As for the two characters "manifestation" (*saṃdarśana*), the text for which appears at the beginning while the intent runs through what follows below; that is, ultimate merit serves as the agent of manifestation.

The profound merit is that which is revealed. Within this revelation of the meaning, there are two aspects each for both exposition (*deśanā*) and practice (*bhāvanā*), distinguished as the agent and the object.
However, the intent of this chapter is extremely profound; previous interpreters have misunderstood it from beginning to end, resulting in a loss of its essential points.

Therefore, I shall first set forth the general meaning of the textual passages concerning the two aspects each of exposition and practice, followed by a detailed commentary according to the topical divisions, so that they may be easily understood. Now, as...
He preaches the Dharma. In the practice of Bodhisattvas, everything is revealed as ultimately profound.
Within the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, the sutra texts explicitly state that he is able to demonstrate and distinguish the ultimate nature of the preaching of the Dharma.

Yet, through the two characters "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā) alone, he constantly manifests his profoundly deep merit. Regarding the practice of Bodhisattvas within the sutra texts, there is a brief mention of practicing the mundane.
The ultimate perfection of merit (referring to "all merits" in the sutra) is because the profound merit is extensively revealed through constant cultivation.

While the Tathāgata’s teaching extensively clarifies analytical exposition, the Bodhisattva’s practice extensively clarifies constant cultivation; consequently, the meaning of the text becomes difficult to perceive.
For this specific reason, the author of the treatise first demonstrates the meaning and only then explains the text. Regarding "abiding in the Dharma," herein:

I am not capable of it. From beginning to end, this single chapter remains obscure to me. How lamentable! (In this section, I shall directly explain the fundamental meaning without distinguishing between divergent interpretations; those who require them may consult the detailed analysis.
Second, the explanation based on the commentary has two parts. First, the section beginning with "The first" uses the teaching of differentiation to manifest the teaching of permanence.

Within this, the "ultimate nature of the Dharma" refers to what the World-Honored One stated regarding the ultimate benefit, as well as the extensive explanation of the Tathāgata’s teaching of differentiation that follows.

Within the ultimate nature of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*), the scriptural text is for the sake of distinguishing [the teachings] according to the capacities of sentient beings; once those capacities are exhausted, it ceases. Therefore, it is "ultimate.

This, in turn, reveals that the Tathāgata’s unconditioned great compassion constantly and uninterruptedly proclaims profound merits; hence it is said that "it is not a teaching based on discrimination," and so forth.
Second, regarding the manifestation of constant cultivation through worldly cultivation: as for the phrase "The second," the first part provides the formal explanation. It says:

Regarding the phrase "cultivating worldly [virtues] and so forth": since the preceding two sections (the second and third) clarified mundane and supramundane merits, this section now refers to them collectively as "all merits.

Because the Dharma adapts to the capacities of beings, it has already been fully demonstrated—within the context of conventional truth—that these are the meritorious qualities of the Bodhisattva’s practices.

(The preceding mundane and supramundane merits both pertain to the two truths; however, because they were taught here specifically as instructions for practice according to capacity, it is said that the "mundane merits" are finalized. Thus it is.

"Coming in accordance with the capacity" is also termed "discriminative exposition. Herein, the previously mentioned methods of practice are integrated; to constantly accord with the one mind is what constitutes constant cultivation. This is based on the principle that phenomena are themselves reality (*tathatā*). Thus, the Sūtra says: "Regarding all merits, one should always maintain a single mind," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "to manifest the remainder" (*ādi*), this refers back [to what precedes]. Among all merits, it manifests that one should always be single-mindedly in accord with principle; thus, it is profound.
Furthermore, because it subsequently explains at length the seven kinds of characteristics of cultivation, it says "the remainder. Question: Now you speak of cultivating worldly merits;
how is it known that these belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)? Answer: As in the aforementioned section on wisdom, by means of reality...

The "locus of meaning" (also called the locus of the ultimate meaning) is contrasted with worldly affairs; this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is elucidated in contrast to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Now, because one constantly cultivates worldly merits by means of the mind of the ultimate meaning, it should be known that these are merits as defined within the context of the conventional truth. However, the preceding sutra provides instruction according to specific matters, and thus speaks of the conventional truth.

Prior to the assembly, there are the two kinds of merit from cultivation: ultimate and profound. Throughout the preceding sections concerning the mundane and supramundane, the sutras each describe these two kinds of cultivation;
it is not merely a matter of appearances, but requires that one constantly accords with principle and returns to the truth through phenomena.
Regarding these various merits, this refers to the second and third sections mentioned above. Since one constantly cultivates with a single mind amidst all these merits, therefore—
It is said that each cultivates two kinds [of practice].

There are two parts to the commentary on the text. First, a brief indication of the two. Regarding "Among these... and so forth: the first is the cultivation of the mundane as an indication of constant cultivation;

this means to constantly accord with the one mind. However, since the Sūtra commands that one should always maintain a single mind regarding all merits, it constitutes the creation through phenomena (sajja-saṃskāra).
Regarding the principle: it was stated above that within each individual category, one cultivates two kinds of meanings and principles. Here, "distancing" refers to being similar to what is below;

that is, this practice causes one to distance oneself [from those lower states], which is the entry into realization. If one constantly accords with the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this is realized wisdom (*jñāna*).
If it is by means of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it merely takes the transformation of images as its object; although it resembles a single mind, it is not truly a single mind.
This is like seeing smoke and knowing there is fire; therefore, it is called "practice resembling a single mind" (this does not mean excluding delusion or the indeterminate, as those are too coarse).

As for "practice contrary to the single mind," this refers to any practice that does not accord with true principle but instead cultivates separate, mundane activities—all such are termed "contrary practices" (this does not refer to greed or hatred).

It is recorded [in the scriptures]. These are all not called "formations" (*saṃskāra*); thus, they are also too coarse [to be so classified]. These formations that are similar yet contradictory are all termed "heedlessness" (*pramāda*).

They are both like enemies and thieves; therefore, one should always admonish oneself to abandon them with a single-minded focus. This meaning is the same as what follows: regarding the attainment of cessation through the Buddha-body, it is like curing a malignant disease or killing an enemy thief.
Furthermore, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) contradict the principle [of reality], they are metaphorically likened to enemies and thieves. [One] removes the one...

This is also the intended meaning [of the passage]: apart from the true reality (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra. Regarding the phrase "without limit" (*amita*) and below: the two types of analytical exposition express the meaning of "constant teaching.

Because of great compassion without object (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*), one is always able to act universally for the sake of sentient beings; it must be without boundaries or limits. This is the meaning of "constant teaching" (that is, constantly performing benefit).

However, because the transformative activities of a single period (*kalpa*) reach their conclusion, it is called "limited and ultimate" (*paricchinna-niṣṭhā*). Nevertheless, the Sūtra cites the "Great... [to indicate that this does not apply to the Buddha].

"Compassion" (*karuṇā*) indicates what is constantly taught. It clearly demonstrates that the analytical teaching of the Dharma according to the capacities of beings is ultimately consummate. This concludes by manifesting the ultimate nature of what was taught in the preceding sutra.

Second, the extensive explanation has two parts. Next, "Furthermore... and so forth. First, regarding the constant cultivation of the seven aspects: these are all intended to cause the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*) to be cultivated.
The "empty marsh within" refers to the very limit of water. "True reality without dualistic thought" refers to the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*).

Because the presence of dualistic thought means it is not the mind of the ultimate truth, the phrase "cultivating so as to bring it before one" means causing it to accord with reality and manifest clearly.
Regarding the six [stages], what is meant by "resting in a state that resembles the Dharma" refers precisely to the aforementioned state where the mind resembles the Dharma.
However, this is known through wisdom alone; in reality, one has not yet seen the Truths (satya). It is like inferring fire from smoke or knowing a pond upon seeing a crane.
Because one allows the mind to find rest therein, it is called "resting in a state that resembles the Dharma. By means of this, one distances oneself from the higher and supreme [realization].

This refers to the "mind of meaning" (*yixin*). Since one does not practice authentically, death will be of no benefit; it is a death in vain (this can be understood by contrasting it with the erroneous interpretations regarding the abiding of dharmas).

The rest is self-evident. Regarding the subsequent section on "extensive explanation," there are two types of "distinctive explanations. This text explicitly states "distinctive explanation," yet both commentaries label them as "constant explanation.

Why do they thus subvert the public good for their private interests? It is because they fail to understand that the Buddha’s teaching was ultimately adapted to the capacities of his listeners, and they instead [misinterpret] it.

Thus he always speaks of great compassion that is without conditions. Within this, the method of transformation is like a physician treating a disease: if one takes the medicine, the illness is removed;

likewise, if one applies mindfulness, it is clearly remembered without forgetting, whereby one attains the Dharma of liberation. It is like a guide showing the way: one reaches the destination ahead. Regarding these matters, the Tathāgata is without fault;
whether one attains benefit or suffers loss depends on whether the sentient being takes and practices [the teaching] or not. Furthermore—
The Buddha does not fail sentient beings. If one does not sincerely practice the worldly dharmas, it is the person themselves who fails the Buddha; how could the Buddha ever fail them?

(This chapter concludes by clarifying that practicing according to this sutra accords with the principle. The profound purport of the Mahāyāna is to abide in the Dharma; to be muddled and thus to deceive both oneself and others is a transgression no small matter.)
V. Displaying the Section on the Certainty of Entry into Realization (Praveśa-niścaya) has three parts. First, the heading.

The treatise does not conclude the preceding section, but merely presents this heading because the meaning—that what was previously cultivated is subsequently realized—is easy to perceive. Since the previous cultivation involved the cessation and path [truths] to treat suffering and its origin, this section follows next to address the certainty of entry into realization.
Second, citing the sutra; third, the commentary’s explanation, which has two parts. Regarding the first, the general [heading], the treatise says: [The text continues with the specific commentary.]
"Manifesting entry and realization" refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths. "Resolving doubts" means that the sutra is definitive and free from uncertainty.

Second, the detailed explanation: [The text says] "Among these," etc. First, the heading of the section; second, the explanation based on it, which has three parts. First, the section on manifesting through skillful means, which has two parts.
[The section on] "Expedient Means" (upāya). First, the intention of the gateway is shown. Because it is the Buddha’s expedient means, he raises the Four Truths to question and reveal [the meaning].

This is because they are the true dharmas; "true" (satya) is the meaning of "truth" (satya). Second, the explanation of the scriptural text has two parts. Regarding "That which... and so forth: first, the object of observation and its basis are revealed.
As for the phrase "should be observed," truth (satya) has two meanings: first, the sense of being real and true. This refers to the object of observation, namely—

Because it does not deviate from the characteristics as they have been described, because it is real, and because it is definitive—namely, that both mundane and supramundane causes and effects are necessarily non-deceptive and cannot be erroneous—this refers to the meaning of "thoroughly examined" (*parīkṣita*). This is in terms of the observing wisdom;

for when noble wisdom observes them, it examines them and finds them to be non-deceptive. Although ordinary beings possess suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), these are not thoroughly examined or real, and thus cannot be so designated.
They are "truths" (*satya*). Because they are known with certainty by non-erroneous noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) regarding their objects, they are called "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).

Due to these two meanings, practitioners constantly observe them. Regarding the statement that "practice arises based upon them," there are both general and specific senses. In the general sense, it means that based on the Four Truths, one gives rise to the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*):
namely, based on the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), one gives rise to the four aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; based on the Truth of Origination...
The Truths: one contemplates the four aspects of arising, origin, production, and condition; the four aspects of cessation, extinction, tranquility, and renunciation;

and the four aspects of path, correctness, practice, and deliverance (also known as the sixteen aspects, which are explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and were briefly cited previously).

Specifically, this refers to the contemplative practices of opposition and conformity based on the Four Noble Truths mentioned below. When the Sūtra speaks of the "Four Truths, suffering and so forth," it refers to oppression (*pīḍana*).

First is contemplation through investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*); second is contemplation according to reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*). The present sutra refers to this as "the clarity of wisdom," which is precisely contemplation according to reality.

This is because it eradicates the root of the views of "self" and "mine. This "root" refers to the "darkness of various delusions" mentioned in the sutra, which is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

By means of this, the subtle, co-emergent afflictions are extinguished; for if these afflictions remain, the views of "self" and "mine" will not be forgotten. Therefore, it is said that "it eradicates the views of self and mine."

This refers to the cessation of the darkness of ignorance through wisdom; it is named the "fundament of self and what belongs to self" because the darkness of ignorance itself constitutes the fundament of self and what belongs to self.

Regarding "the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are unreal," this is the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

First, the textual lineage of this sutra is as orderly as a string of pearls. It is precisely because previous scholars have broken the text into fragments and provided separate explanations that they have frequently missed the profound intent of the sutra and its treatises.

"Self-nature, three. The Commentary states below: First, it clarifies how the single mind treats various self-natures.

Since it is a false conceptualization that calculates the existence of a self-nature, therefore—
This refers to the obstacle of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The antidote to this obstacle is solely the mind of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*):

This refers to the true wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Since all phenomena are fundamentally empty, there is nothing with which they can be contrasted.

If one were to consider them in terms of relative antidotes, because that which is to be remedied is impermanent, the remedy itself must also be impermanent; thus it is said that "all things that exist as relative antidotes are impermanent.

This is like the relationship between the subject and object of remediation within the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), which applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Since the remediation of the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) already exists...
These are designated as having characteristics (*sanimitta*) and are entirely impermanent (*anitya*). This applies not only to worldly, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena;

because he had previously urged those with doubts to ask their questions, and since the first watch of the night had not yet passed—having reached the middle watch—he was about to enter parinirvāṇa. Even if there were further doubts, the time [was now past].

However, all other sutras conclude with verses on the circulation [of the Dharma], such as "When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra," and so forth; this one does not.
This has two meanings. First, as for why other sūtras conclude with a statement on circulation:

because the Buddha’s teaching for that particular occasion was finished, it was necessary to conclude it in order to distinguish it from what was taught at other times. Now, having completed the explicit exposition of this sūtra, there is no further teaching;
thus, it differs from other occasions where a concluding distinction is made. Second, the final four phrases alone constitute the conclusion.
The text states: "He cautioned his disciples not to speak, fearing they might miss the hour of midnight, and said, 'The time is nearly past;
I wish to enter parinirvāṇa. Although this was intended as a caution against speaking, it thereby reveals that he was entering extinction at that moment.
Furthermore, he said, 'This is my final instruction,' which shows that nothing more would be spoken thereafter. Therefore, the compilers of the canon extracted these four phrases."

The intent is as follows: In the introductory section, it was first stated that "at this time, the midnight was tranquil and silent," in order to exhort the assembly and urge them to listen attentively.
Therefore, the meaning of the first two lines is no different from that of the subsequent four lines;

However, because this sutra was taught by the Tathāgata as a final instruction at the time of his passing, it has been lectured upon every year during the middle spring to repay his virtue.

Regarding the arrival of Master Kumārajīva’s translations: because the meaning of the Mahāyāna was obscured, people treated it as merely a "small vehicle" (Hīnayāna).

Aśvaghoṣa, foreseeing this, subsequently composed treatises to explain it. Paramārtha translated them during the Chen dynasty, but they were only widely disseminated after a long time; he then began to translate the sūtras and śāstras.
